units.title: Rhetorical Situation
units.blurb: Exigence, audience, occasion and purpose, the appeals of ethos, pathos, logos and kairos, and tone, diction and register. The choices the rhetorical analysis essay asks you to name and explain.
keys: Exigence is the urgent problem that makes a writer speak now, while occasion is the specific event or setting where the text is delivered.
Audience is described by its values, beliefs and assumptions, and a hostile or undecided audience demands common ground before the claim.
Purpose is stated as an infinitive verb plus an audience effect, such as to warn, to unify, to satirize, to justify or to mobilize.
Ethos is granted by the audience, pathos names a specific emotion, logos lives in the reasoning behind a number, and kairos seizes the moment.
Tone is the writer's attitude named with a precise adjective and proven by diction, while mood is the feeling produced in the reader.
Diction is analyzed in clusters, and connotation, register and the pivot from concrete to abstract words carry the hidden argument.
Concession followed by refutation earns trust and reclaims ground, and a qualifier like often or unless makes a claim harder to disprove.
Commentary runs choice, effect on the specific audience, purpose, and naming a device without explaining its effect earns no Row B credit.

topics.t: Audience beliefs, values, needs and backgrounds
Perceptions of the audience guide choices
Relating to an audience's emotions and values
Comparisons that relate to an audience
Syntax and diction shape how the writer is perceived

excl.s: The CED names no required texts and no required literary or grammatical terminology; the exam assesses the skills and essential knowledge, not term recall.

frq.title: Rhetorical analysis: a food bank director asks growers to open their fields
frq.stem:
In the fall of 2025, the director of a regional food bank, who grew up on a family farm in the county, spoke at the annual dinner of the county farm bureau, an audience of commercial growers. The food bank was launching a program to glean (harvest and collect) crops that farmers leave unpicked when market prices fall below the cost of harvesting them. The passage below is an excerpt from that speech. (The speaker and speech are invented for practice; an exam passage runs 600 to 800 words.)

Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices the director makes to persuade the growers to open their fields to the gleaning program.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices.
• Select and use evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Demonstrate an understanding of the rhetorical situation.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

My father used to say that a farmer is the only person who can lose money by having a good year. Most of you have lived that sentence. When the price of sweet corn drops below what it costs to pay a picker, the smart decision is to leave it standing. I have made that decision myself, at the edge of my family's field with a calculator in my hand, and I would make it again. So I am not here tonight to tell you that you are wasting food. You are running businesses, and nobody in this room can afford a kindness that does not pencil out.

But I want to tell you where that corn could go.

Last year the food bank served 11,400 households in this county, a third more than the year before. Our shelves are full of what keeps: canned soup, boxed pasta, peanut butter. What we almost never have is anything that grew here. In August a mother in Linden told one of our volunteers that her children had not eaten a fresh vegetable since school let out. She lives four miles from some of the best farmland in the state.

Here is what we are proposing. You tell us which rows you are leaving. We bring the crews (students, church groups, retirees who miss the work) and we bring the insurance. We pick what the market will not pay you to pick, we haul it away, and we hand you a receipt for the tax deduction. You lose nothing you had not already written off. Your field is cleared for fall tillage. And a family in Linden gets tomatoes.

Some of you are thinking that you have heard promises like this before, from people in town who have never driven a tractor. Fair enough. Judge us by the pilot. Last September three farms on Route 9 let us in. In six weekends we gleaned forty-one thousand pounds of produce. Not one of those farmers lost a day of work, and all three have signed up again.

Farmers have always shared the harvest. Your grandparents called it threshing season: every family on the road brought their hands to your field, and you brought yours to theirs. Nobody sent a bill, and nobody went without. That is all this is. It is threshing season with a food bank truck at the end of the row.

There is a sign-up sheet on every table tonight. Put down one field. One row. And next August, when my father's sentence comes true again and the price drops below the cost of picking, you will know exactly where that corn can go.

rows.earns: A defensible thesis that analyzes the director's rhetorical choices in light of her purpose and these growers, for example: 'Speaking as a farmer's daughter to growers wary of town charity, the director concedes that leaving crops unpicked is sound business, proves her program costs them nothing, and recasts gleaning as the threshing-season tradition their grandparents kept, so that giving becomes both good business and inherited duty.' The thesis may be more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('the director uses rhetorical choices to persuade the farmers'); naming appeals with no purpose ('she uses ethos, pathos, and logos'); summarizing the program; or a claim about hunger in general that never addresses the director's choices.

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning (the father's saying, the calculator at the field's edge, 'a kindness that does not pencil out,' 11,400 households, the Linden mother four miles from farmland, 'You lose nothing you had not already written off,' the Route 9 pilot, threshing season, 'one field. One row.') and commentary consistently explains how each choice answers these growers' beliefs and needs (profit, suspicion of outsiders, pride in tradition) and so advances the director's purpose, showing how several choices work together.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence throughout, but commentary explains only some choices or ties them unevenly to the growers. 2: some specific evidence, but commentary mostly restates it, or no line of reasoning holds the paragraphs together. 1: mostly general evidence and summary of the speech. 0: restates the thesis, repeats the passage, or is irrelevant. Labeling the Linden mother 'pathos' without naming the feeling (discomfort at hunger beside their own fields) and why it moves business owners stays at 2 or below.

rows.earns: A consistently complex understanding of the rhetorical situation, for example explaining the tension the director must manage (asking profit-minded growers for charity without calling them wasteful or naive) and how the concession, the tax receipt, and the threshing-season tradition resolve it; or explaining the significance of the frame, the father's complaint about good years returning at the end as the reason to act; or a style that is consistently vivid and persuasive.
rows.loses: A single sentence calling the speech 'very effective'; a sweeping statement about hunger in America; a complex idea mentioned once and dropped; or elevated vocabulary that does not carry an insight. The point is awarded for the whole essay's thinking, not for one clever sentence.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that earns the point.
parts.a: Model: 'Addressing growers who expect to be lectured by town charities, the director first speaks as one of them, conceding that leaving corn unpicked is the rational choice; she then makes the program cost-free and proven, and finally recasts gleaning as the threshing-season sharing their grandparents practiced, so that opening their fields feels like both good business and family tradition.' It names the audience's belief, three choices in order, and the purpose they serve.
parts.n: 'The director uses ethos, pathos, and logos to persuade the farmers' restates the prompt with a device list and earns nothing.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs in a line of reasoning, each with evidence and the commentary that earns the points.
parts.a:
¶1 Disarming the audience: 'I have made that decision myself, at the edge of my family's field with a calculator' and 'nobody in this room can afford a kindness that does not pencil out.' Commentary: she speaks as a grower, granting that leaving corn is rational, which removes the accusation of waste the audience expects and earns a hearing for 'But I want to tell you where that corn could go.'
¶2 Answering the business and the skeptic: the 'you tell us / we bring' division of labor, the tax receipt, 'You lose nothing you had not already written off,' then the Route 9 pilot (six weekends, forty-one thousand pounds, all three farms signed up again). Commentary: each detail answers a grower's question (what does it cost me? will it disrupt my work? have you done this before?), and 'Fair enough' concedes their distrust of 'people in town' before local proof answers it.
¶3 Turning business into belonging: the Linden mother 'four miles from some of the best farmland in the state' and 'threshing season with a food bank truck at the end of the row.' Commentary: the irony of hunger beside their fields creates discomfort, and the tradition lets growers give as neighbors rather than as donors; the closing return to the father's sentence and 'One field. One row.' make the request small and immediate.
parts.n: Paragraphs organized by appeal ('ethos paragraph, pathos paragraph') tend to list; organize by what the director does to the audience, in the passage's order.

parts.q: Row C plan: name one way this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Develop the central tension throughout: the director must ask business owners for generosity without insulting their business sense. Show that each move reconciles the two (the concession honors their judgment, the tax receipt keeps the gift inside their ledger, threshing season makes sharing a farm custom rather than town charity), and explain the frame's significance: the father's sentence, first a complaint about bad markets, returns as the growers' chance to make a good year count.
parts.n: Tacking 'this speech is relevant to hunger everywhere' onto the conclusion is not sophistication; the complexity must be argued through the essay.

frq.title: Argument: should a speaker say the same thing to every audience?
frq.stem:
In a widely shared essay, a veteran high school debate coach wrote: 'Someone who says exactly the same thing to every audience is not principled. They are simply not listening.' (The coach and essay are invented for practice.)

Write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which a speaker or writer should adapt what they say to the audience.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
• Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

rows.earns: A defensible position on how far a speaker should adapt, for example: 'A speaker should adapt how a claim is made (evidence, examples, register) to every audience, but one who changes the claim itself to please each audience has stopped arguing and started campaigning.' Agreeing, disagreeing, or qualifying the coach's claim can all earn the point.
rows.loses: Restating the coach's claim; 'some people adapt and some do not'; 'it depends on the situation' with no position; or an obvious fact ('audiences are different').

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence from reading, history, current events, or experience supports every claim in a line of reasoning (a doctor explaining one diagnosis to a frightened child and to a colleague; a candidate who promises opposite things in two towns; a company apology that tells investors one story and customers another), and commentary consistently explains how each example proves the essay's distinction or claim.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence, but commentary explains only some of it. 2: some specific evidence, but commentary mostly restates it, or there is no clear line of reasoning. 1: general or hypothetical evidence with little explanation ('for example, if someone talked to kids...'). 0: restates the thesis or is irrelevant. Examples that are listed without saying what each proves stay at 2 or below.

rows.earns: A nuanced argument that consistently explores the tension, for example distinguishing adapting expression from adapting position, then conceding that genuine listening sometimes should change the position itself (new evidence from the audience) and explaining how to tell honest revision from pandering; or situating the question in a broader context such as public trust in institutions; or a consistently vivid, persuasive style.
rows.loses: 'This is a complex issue' with no development; a counterargument named in one sentence and dropped; or a conclusion that claims nuance the body never shows.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that earns the point.
parts.a: Model: 'The coach is right that refusing to adapt is a failure to listen, but only about the manner of an argument: a speaker should change evidence, examples, and tone for each audience while keeping the claim itself constant, because a claim that changes with every room is no longer a conviction but a sales pitch.'
parts.n: 'The coach makes an interesting point about audiences' takes no position and earns nothing.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs with specific evidence and commentary.
parts.a:
¶1 Adapting manner serves the truth: a pediatrician tells a frightened seven-year-old that the cast is 'a suit of armor for the bone' and tells a colleague 'a displaced distal radius fracture.' Commentary: the diagnosis is identical; only the language changes, and the child's understanding is the proof that adapting served, rather than bent, the truth.
¶2 Adapting the claim betrays both audiences: a candidate promises a factory town to protect coal jobs and a city fundraiser to phase coal out. Commentary: each audience hears what it wants, but when the two speeches meet online, both lose trust, showing that changing the position is not listening but pandering.
¶3 Where listening should change the claim: a principal proposes a phone ban, hears students describe using phones to reach working parents, and revises the rule to allow calls at lunch. Commentary: the claim changed because the audience supplied evidence, not because the principal wanted applause; the test is whether the change answers new evidence or merely new listeners.
parts.n: Evidence need not come from famous sources, but it must be specific and each example must be explained; three examples with no commentary score as 1 or 2.

parts.q: Row C plan: name one way this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Build the whole essay on the distinction between manner and position, then complicate it in paragraph 3: listening can legitimately change a position, so the essay proposes a test (does the change answer new evidence or only a new audience?) and uses it to judge each example. Close by explaining why the distinction matters now, when every speech to one audience can be replayed to all the others.
parts.n: A closing sentence saying 'both sides have a point' is equivocation, not nuance.

frq.title: Synthesis: should high schools require a course in public speaking?
frq.stem:
Surveys regularly find that public speaking is among the fears adults report most often, and employers regularly list oral communication among the skills they value most. Some school districts now require every student to complete a semester course in public speaking before graduation; others offer it only as an elective, citing students' anxiety and crowded schedules.

Carefully read the following six sources, including the introductory information for each source. Write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on whether high schools should require every student to complete a course in public speaking.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
• Select and use evidence from at least three of the provided sources to support your line of reasoning. Indicate clearly the sources used through direct quotation, paraphrase, or summary. Sources may be cited as Source A, Source B, etc., or by using the description in parentheses.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

(All six sources, their authors, and their figures are invented for practice and summarized here; on the exam each text source runs about 500 words and two sources are visual.)

Source A (Okafor, education journal)
Maya Okafor, a professor of communication, 'Speaking Is Taught, Not Born,' an article in a journal for secondary teachers, 2023. Okafor argues that confident speakers are made by practice and feedback rather than born with a gift, and that the students who most fear speaking are those who have practiced least. In her study of four high schools, students who completed a required semester course rated their speaking anxiety lower at the end than at the start. She concludes that an optional course lets the most anxious students avoid exactly the practice they need.

Source B (business council chart)
A bar chart from a report by a regional business council, 2024, titled 'Skills employers rate as very important in new hires (percent of 600 employers).' The horizontal axis lists five skills; the vertical axis runs from 0 to 100 percent. Bar heights: Oral communication 78 · Teamwork 74 · Written communication 71 · Problem solving 69 · Technical skills 52. A note beneath the chart states that only 31 percent of the same employers rated recent graduates' oral communication as 'strong.'

Source C (Reyes, student op-ed)
Daniel Reyes, a high school senior, 'Don't Make Us Perform,' an op-ed in his school newspaper, 2024. Reyes, who describes his own social anxiety, argues that a required speech course would punish quiet students for their temperament and make school a place of dread. He proposes alternatives that build the same skills: recorded video presentations, small-group discussions, and one-on-one conferences with teachers. 'Communication,' he writes, 'is not the same thing as performance.'

Source D (district curriculum memo)
A memo from the curriculum office of a suburban school district to its school board, 2024. Adding a required semester of public speaking would need about six additional class sections per high school each year; with no new funding, roughly one in five students would lose an elective (the memo names a second year of art or of computer science). Only two teachers in the district hold a speech certification.

Source E (Lindqvist, civic essay)
Karin Lindqvist, a former city council member, 'The Empty Microphone,' an essay in a civic affairs magazine, 2022. Lindqvist describes years of public hearings at which the same few residents spoke while hundreds stayed silent, and argues that decisions made in those rooms favored the people comfortable at the microphone. Teaching every student to speak in public, she contends, is a matter of democratic fairness, not career preparation.

Source F (Brandt, psychology article)
Lena Brandt, a clinical psychologist, 'Exposure Without Ambush,' an article on a popular psychology website, 2023. Brandt explains that gradual, supported exposure to a feared situation reduces anxiety for most people, but that forced, high-stakes exposure without preparation can deepen avoidance. She recommends that any speaking requirement begin with low-stakes tasks, let students set their own goals, and grade growth rather than polish.

rows.earns: A defensible position on whether schools should require the course, for example: 'High schools should require public speaking, but as a graduated course that grades growth rather than polish, because the skill is learned, scarce, and essential to civic fairness, and only a requirement reaches the students who would otherwise avoid it.' Arguing against a requirement, or for a modified one, can equally earn the point.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt; 'there are pros and cons to requiring public speaking'; 'public speaking is an important skill' (an obvious fact, not a claim); or a summary of the sources with no position.

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence from at least three sources, clearly cited (Source A or 'Okafor'), supports every claim in a line of reasoning, and commentary consistently explains how each piece supports it: Okafor's finding that the most anxious practice least argues for requiring, not offering; the chart's gap between 78 percent 'very important' and 31 percent 'strong' shows an unmet need; Lindqvist extends the stakes beyond jobs to fairness; Reyes and Brandt are answered as a design problem rather than a reason to refuse.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence from three sources, but commentary explains only some of it. 2: evidence from three sources, but explanation is limited or there is no line of reasoning. 1: evidence from at least two sources, summarized rather than explained. 0: restates the thesis, only summarizes, or references fewer than two sources. Citing only the chart's 78 percent without its 31 percent note misses what the chart argues.

rows.earns: A nuanced argument that consistently works the tensions among sources, for example showing that Okafor and Brandt agree practice reduces fear but disagree on whether pressure helps, and that this disagreement shapes the kind of requirement the essay proposes; or weighing Source D's real cost (a lost art or computer science elective) against Source E's civic stakes; or explaining a limitation of the sources (a four-school study, a regional survey); or a consistently vivid, persuasive style.
rows.loses: One sentence acknowledging that 'some students are anxious'; a counterargument named once and dropped; or listing the sources' disagreements without using them to shape the position.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that earns the point.
parts.a: Model: 'High schools should require every student to take public speaking, because the skill is learned rather than innate, employers find it scarce, and civic life rewards those who can use a microphone; but the requirement should be built as graduated practice that grades growth, since a course designed as a performance would teach anxious students to fear speaking more.'
parts.n: 'Public speaking is an important skill for students' states an obvious fact and takes no position on the requirement.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs, naming the sources each uses and the commentary that ties them to the line of reasoning.
parts.a:
¶1 The skill is learned and the need is real (Sources A, B): Okafor's study shows anxiety falling after a required course and her point that the most fearful practice least; the chart shows 78 percent of employers call oral communication very important while only 31 percent find graduates strong. Commentary: the gap is a teaching gap, and an elective leaves it to the students least likely to close it.
¶2 The stakes are civic, not only economic (Source E, with B): Lindqvist's silent hearings show that people uncomfortable at the microphone lose influence over decisions. Commentary: if speaking is a skill of citizenship, a requirement is a matter of fairness, as a civics course is, not a job-training option.
¶3 The objection becomes the design (Sources C, F, D): Reyes's fear and his line that communication is not performance, Brandt's warning that ambush exposure deepens avoidance, and her remedy of low-stakes tasks and graded growth; Source D's staffing cost. Commentary: the evidence argues against a performance-first course, not against a requirement, so the course should start with small groups and recorded talks; the cost is real, but training existing teachers is cheaper than leaving the gap Source B measures.
parts.n: Summarizing each source in turn ('Source A says... Source B says...') without tying it to the thesis is the classic Row B score of 1 or 2.

parts.q: Row C plan: name one way this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Make the tension between Okafor and Brandt the engine of the essay: both say practice reduces fear, but Okafor trusts a requirement to supply it while Brandt warns that pressure can backfire, so the essay's position (require it, but grade growth) is built from their disagreement. Acknowledge the limitation that Okafor studied only four schools and the chart surveys one region, and explain why the argument still holds.
parts.n: Adding 'however, some people disagree' in the conclusion is not complexity; the tension has to shape the position throughout.

frq.title: Reading set: a fire chief's letter about closing a station
frq.stem:
The following passage is a letter published in a rural township's newsletter in 2025. Its writer, the township's volunteer fire chief, was responding to the township board's proposal to close the fire station on the north side of the township to save money. (The letter and its writer are invented for practice.)

(1) I have been a volunteer firefighter in this township for twenty-six years, and I have never before written a letter to this newsletter. (2) I am writing now because on Monday the township board will vote on whether to close Station 2, and you deserve to know what that vote means before it happens.

(3) I understand why the board is looking for savings. (4) Every one of us has watched the tax bill climb, and nobody on the board wants to raise it again. (5) But closing Station 2 is not a savings. (6) It is a bet. (7) From Station 1, our trucks need nineteen minutes to reach the homes along Ridge Road; from Station 2, they need six. (8) Our training manuals warn that a room fire in a modern house can go from a spark to fully engulfed in about five minutes. (9) The board is betting that nothing on Ridge Road will ever burn.

(10) Some of you have told me that Station 2 is only a garage with two old trucks. (11) You are right about the trucks. (12) But a fire station is less like a garage than like a smoke detector: you resent the chirp of its battery until the night it wakes you.

(13) I am not asking you to take my word for any of this. (14) Come to the board meeting on Monday at seven. (15) Ask the board for the response times. (16) Then ask them which families on Ridge Road they have told.

parts.q:
Which of the following best describes the writer's exigence?
(A) The steady rise in the township's tax bill
(B) The board's upcoming vote on whether to close Station 2
(C) Residents' complaints about the condition of the trucks
(D) The writer's twenty-six years of volunteer service
parts.a: (B). Sentence 2 names the prompt for writing: 'on Monday the township board will vote on whether to close Station 2.' (A) is the board's motive, which the writer grants in sentence 4, not his reason for writing; (C) is an objection he answers in sentences 10 and 11; (D) is his credential, and sentence 1 says it never before led him to write.
parts.n: RHS-1.B, skill 1.A. Distractors name real details from the letter; the exigence is the event that made this letter necessary now.

parts.q:
Sentence 1 primarily serves to
(A) establish the writer's credibility and signal that the occasion is unusually serious
(B) criticize residents who have never volunteered
(C) summarize the history of the township's fire department
(D) apologize in advance for the length of the letter
parts.a: (A). Twenty-six years of service gives him standing on the subject, and 'I have never before written a letter' tells readers that only something grave could prompt him to write, which introduces both the writer and the stakes before the subject is named. Nothing in the sentence blames residents (B), recounts department history (C), or apologizes (D).
parts.n: RHS-1.I, skill 1.A. An introduction may introduce the writer as well as the subject; credentials plus a break from habit do both.

parts.q:
In sentences 3 and 4, the writer acknowledges the board's reason for the proposal primarily in order to
(A) concede that closing Station 2 is the right decision
(B) show that he understands the readers' concern about taxes before disputing the board's reasoning
(C) suggest that the board members are dishonest about the budget
(D) introduce a proposal to raise taxes
parts.a: (B). 'Every one of us has watched the tax bill climb' places the writer among taxpaying readers and grants the legitimacy of the concern, so the 'But' in sentence 5 reads as a fair correction rather than a dismissal. He does not accept the closure (A), accuse anyone of dishonesty (C), or propose a tax (D).
parts.n: RHS-1.F, skill 1.B. Acknowledging an audience's value is not agreement with the conclusion; the turn at 'But' is the tell.

parts.q:
The comparison in sentence 12 relies chiefly on the readers'
(A) technical knowledge of firefighting equipment
(B) familiarity with an everyday device that seems a nuisance until it saves a life
(C) memory of a particular fire on Ridge Road
(D) respect for the members of the township board
parts.a: (B). Nearly every reader owns a smoke detector and knows the annoyance of its low-battery chirp, so the comparison converts 'only a garage' into something they already value despite its costs, which is how a shared comparison advances the writer's purpose. It requires no technical knowledge (A), names no past fire (C), and does not invoke the board (D).
parts.n: RHS-1.K, skill 1.B. An effective comparison must be shared and understood by this audience; ask what the readers already know.

parts.q:
The final paragraph (sentences 13 to 16) functions primarily to
(A) summarize the evidence about response times
(B) move readers from agreement to action by urging them to attend the meeting and question the board
(C) concede that the writer's figures may be mistaken
(D) console residents of Ridge Road for the loss of their station
parts.a: (B). The imperatives 'Come,' 'Ask,' and 'Then ask' call readers to a specific action with a time and place, and the last question turns the reader into the one who holds the board accountable. Sentence 13 invites verification rather than conceding error (C); the paragraph neither summarizes (A) nor consoles (D), since the station has not yet closed.
parts.n: RHS-1.J, skill 1.A. 'I am not asking you to take my word' is confidence, not concession: it hands readers the means to check.

frq.title: Writing set: a student's draft letter to the parks board
frq.stem:
The following passage is a draft of a letter that a high school junior plans to send to the members of her town's parks board, most of whom are retirees who have served on the board for many years. (The draft is invented for practice.)

(1) The town pool on Dale Street has been closed since last August, when the parks board decided that repairing it would cost more than the town could afford. (2) The board's engineer estimated that fixing the pool's cracked concrete basin and its forty-year-old pump would cost 180,000 dollars, nearly a fifth of the parks department's yearly budget. (3) That is a lot of money, and I get why people freaked out about it.

(4) However, the pool was more than a place to swim. (5) For many families on the east side of town, it was the only place where children could spend a long summer afternoon safely and for free. (6) The nearest other public pool is eleven miles away, and many of these families do not own cars. (7) Last summer, attendance at the library's free children's programs doubled, which the librarians attribute partly to the pool's closure.

(8) There are ways to pay for the repairs without raising taxes. (9) The state's Community Recreation Fund offers matching grants that cover up to half the cost of repairing public pools in towns of fewer than 20,000 residents. (10) Local businesses, such as the hardware store and the two banks on Main Street, could sponsor lanes or a youth swim team. (11) And a small daily fee for adults, with children admitted free, would help cover the cost of running the new pump each summer.

(12) The pool is worth saving.

parts.q:
The writer wants to add a sentence before sentence 1 that would both capture the board members' interest and introduce the topic of the letter. Which of the following best achieves this purpose?
(A) Swimming is a healthy form of exercise for people of all ages.
(B) Many of you learned to swim in the Dale Street pool, and some of you taught your own children there.
(C) Pools can be found in towns of every size across the country.
(D) I am a junior at Central High School, and I enjoy swimming.
parts.a: (B). It relates the subject to the board members' own memories and values, engaging retirees who have long ties to the town, while introducing the specific pool the letter is about. (A) and (C) are generalities that could open any letter about pools, and (D) introduces the writer but gives the board no reason to care.
parts.n: RHS-1.I, skill 2.A. The right opening must do both jobs the question names, engage this audience and introduce this topic.

parts.q:
In sentence 3 (reproduced below), the writer wants to acknowledge the board's concern about cost in language appropriate to her audience.
That is a lot of money, and I get why people freaked out about it.
Which version of the underlined portion ('I get why people freaked out about it') best achieves this purpose?
(A) (as it is now)
(B) I understand why the board hesitated to spend it
(C) the board totally overreacted
(D) some people were upset about it, I guess
parts.a: (B). Measured, respectful diction acknowledges the board's decision as reasonable caution, which presents the student as a serious writer and keeps the retirees willing to hear her proposal. (A) and (D) use casual phrasing ('freaked out,' 'I guess') that can make adult readers take her less seriously, and (C) insults the audience she needs to persuade.
parts.n: RHS-1.L, skill 2.B. Diction shapes how this audience perceives the writer and so whether it accepts the argument.

parts.q:
The writer wants to add evidence after sentence 7 that would most effectively show the board members that the pool's closure has put children at risk. Which of the following best achieves this purpose?
(A) Public swimming pools were first built in ancient times.
(B) Last summer the county sheriff's office recorded nine rescues of children swimming in the unsupervised quarry on Mill Road, up from two the summer before.
(C) My friends and I were very disappointed when the pool closed.
(D) Many larger cities have several public pools.
parts.a: (B). A specific, local, official record links the closure to danger in the board's own jurisdiction, evidence that speaks to their responsibility for the town's children. (A) and (D) are irrelevant to this town, and (C) offers feeling rather than proof and centers the writer rather than the children.
parts.n: RHS-1.N, skill 2.B. The best evidence is drawn from this audience's context and answers its needs, not the most emotional or general option.

parts.q:
The writer wants to add a sentence before sentence 8 that addresses a concern the board members are likely to have before she proposes ways to pay for the repairs. Which of the following best achieves this purpose?
(A) I know the board's first duty is to spend taxpayers' money carefully, and I would not ask for a repair the town cannot sustain.
(B) Money should not matter when children are involved.
(C) Budgets are boring, but they are important.
(D) Other parks boards have been braver than this one.
parts.a: (A). It names the board's own value (careful stewardship of public money) and promises that her proposal respects it, so the funding ideas in sentences 8 to 11 are read as responsible rather than naive. (B) dismisses the board's central concern, (C) is flippant, and (D) insults the audience.
parts.n: RHS-1.F, skill 2.B. Showing you understand the audience's concern before making the request is what 'demonstrate understanding of an audience' means.

parts.q:
The writer wants to replace sentence 12 with a conclusion that calls the board to a specific action. Which of the following best achieves this purpose?
(A) (as it is now)
(B) In conclusion, the pool mattered to families, and there are ways to pay for it.
(C) I ask the board to apply for a Community Recreation Fund grant at its next meeting and to set a goal of reopening the Dale Street pool by next June.
(D) Pools have been a part of summer for generations.
parts.a: (C). It names a concrete step, a timeline, and the funding source the letter has just established, so the conclusion turns the argument into a decision the board can make. (A) restates a judgment without an action, (B) summarizes, and (D) drifts into generality.
parts.n: RHS-1.J, skill 2.A. Match the stated goal: a call to act needs a specific action, not a summary or a restated opinion.

units.ced: AP English Language and Composition Course and Exam Description, Effective Fall 2024

units.title: Claims and Evidence
units.blurb: Claims of fact, value and policy, kinds of evidence and their limits, Toulmin warrants and backing, syllogisms and enthymemes, classical and Rogerian arrangement, and a long run of named fallacies with examples.
keys: A defensible thesis takes an arguable stance a reasonable reader could contest, and a precise qualifier narrows it without hedging.
Claims of fact, value, policy, cause and definition carry different burdens, and a claim of cause must rule out other explanations.
Evidence must be relevant, sufficient and accurate, and commentary must explain how it supports the claim rather than summarize it.
Statistics, anecdote, expert testimony, analogy and historical example each have a limit, so strong essays pair a number with a story.
A Toulmin warrant is the unstated assumption that lets data support a claim, and an enthymeme is a syllogism that leaves that premise unstated.
Induction yields a probable conclusion from cases, deduction a necessary one from premises, and a valid syllogism with a false premise is unsound.
Fallacies like straw man, post hoc and false dilemma are analyzed by quoting the words and exposing what the reasoning skips, not by labeling.
Classical arrangement runs exordium, narratio, confirmatio, refutatio and peroratio, while Rogerian argument concedes first to a hostile audience.

units.title: Reasoning and Organization
units.blurb: Lines of reasoning, topic sentences, transitions, methods of development, introductions, conclusions and counterargument placement, plus how the synthesis essay cites and frames prose and visual sources.
keys: A line of reasoning holds when the topic sentences read in order build toward the thesis instead of forming a list that could be reordered.
A body paragraph opens with a topic sentence stating its subclaim, then evidence, at least two sentences of commentary, and a link to the thesis.
Transitions must match the logic the sentences actually perform, and repeated key terms and clear pronoun reference keep a paragraph coherent.
Methods of development like definition or cause-effect and patterns like order of importance are rhetorical choices, not just essay templates.
An introduction narrows to a defensible thesis in three or four sentences, and a conclusion extends the stakes rather than restating the thesis.
The counterargument sits after the strongest paragraphs and before the conclusion, conceded fairly, turned with yet, then substantively refuted.
Synthesis cites at least three sources as (Source C) or with an attributive tag and puts them in conversation around the writer's own claim.
A chart, cartoon or photograph counts as a citable source, and its trend or composition must be analyzed for the claim, not listed as data.

units.title: Style
units.blurb: Schemes and tropes by name, from anaphora and antithesis to metonymy and litotes, plus periodic and cumulative sentences, irony, punctuation for effect, passive voice and the usage rules the writing questions test.
keys: Schemes of repetition are named by position, with anaphora at clause openings, epistrophe at closings, and anadiplosis chaining end to start.
Antithesis sets contrasts in parallel form, antimetabole repeats the same words reversed, and chiasmus reverses only the grammatical shape.
Asyndeton speeds a list and polysyndeton slows it, while a rhetorical question recruits the audience and hypophora answers its own question.
Metaphor asserts, simile compares with like or as, metonymy swaps an associated thing, synecdoche swaps a part, and litotes affirms by negating.
Verbal irony builds complicity with readers who catch the gap, and Juvenalian satire like A Modest Proposal condemns where Horatian amuses.
Periodic sentences delay the main clause for suspense, cumulative ones lead with it, and subordination ranks ideas that coordination equalizes.
A colon promises a payoff and a dash breaks in for emphasis, while passive voice can erase the actor on purpose, as in mistakes were made.
That marks a restrictive clause and which a nonrestrictive one, and comma splices, dangling modifiers and broken parallelism are revision targets.

units.title: Exam Craft
units.blurb: The shape of the exam and how readers score it. Section timing, the synthesis, rhetorical analysis and argument tasks, the thesis, evidence and sophistication rubric rows, and tactics for reading and revision questions.
keys: The exam runs 45 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes for 45 percent, then three essays in 2 hours 15 minutes for 55 percent.
Q1 synthesis cites at least three sources, Q2 analyzes a writer's choices in a given passage, and Q3 argues the student's own position.
Each essay earns 1 point for a defensible thesis, up to 4 for evidence and commentary, and 1 for sophistication, with rows scored independently.
Row B rises from summarized to explained evidence to a full line of reasoning, and sophistication must be sustained, not one closing line.
Defend, challenge and qualify score equally, and a qualified position names the conditions under which the claim holds rather than fence-sitting.
A rhetorical analysis paragraph runs choice, evidence, effect on the specific audience, purpose, and device-hunting caps Row B at 1 or 2.
Budget about 40 minutes per essay, plan the thesis and full topic sentences in five minutes, and switch essays on schedule even if unfinished.
With no guessing penalty on multiple choice, read the stem first, predict an answer, and reject choices true of the passage but off the question.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The rhetorical situation of a text collectively refers to its exigence, purpose, audience, writer, context, and message (the CED's six components). A writer makes every choice, from an appeal to a single word, in response to that situation, so analysis explains a choice by tying it to these components, above all to purpose and audience.
cards.h: → the six components + why choices answer to them
cards.n: Reciting the six terms earns nothing on Q2: the rubric rewards showing how a specific choice answers this writer's purpose and audience.
x: writer, audience, purpose, context, exigence, message
exigence, purpose, audience, writer, context, message

cards.q: Define message in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The message is the central idea or claim a text communicates: what the writer asserts about the subject. It is one of the six components; the other five (exigence, purpose, audience, writer, context) explain why the message is framed as it is, for whom, and to what end.
cards.h: → one-sentence definition + its place among six
cards.n: Stating the message is summary; a Q2 thesis earns the point only when it says how choices convey the message to this audience.

cards.q: Define writer (or speaker) as an element of the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The writer is the person or institution producing the text, together with the identity, experience, expertise, values, and relationship to the audience they bring to it. Those traits shape what the writer can credibly say and how the audience receives it, which is why the exam's headnote identifies the writer.
cards.h: → who + what they bring to the text
cards.n: Biography is not analysis: a detail about the writer earns credit only when tied to a choice it enables, such as an anecdote only this writer could tell.

cards.q: Contrast the author and the speaker of a text.
cards.a: The author is the real person who wrote the text; the speaker is the voice or persona constructed inside it. Usually they align, but an author may adopt a speaker whose views or tone differ from their own, as in satire, so analysis attributes choices to the author and attitudes to the speaker.
cards.n: Reading a satirical narrator's proposal as the author's sincere view inverts the purpose; ask whose voice is speaking and what the author wants us to think of it.

cards.q: Recall what each letter of SOAPSTone stands for.
cards.a: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone. It is a classroom checklist, not CED language: the CED's rhetorical situation is exigence, purpose, audience, writer, context, and message, so add exigence and message when you use it to read a passage.
cards.h: → six words, then what it leaves out
cards.n: SOAPSTone is not in the CED; using its letters as essay paragraphs produces a list, not a line of reasoning.
x: Speaker Occasion Audience Purpose Subject Tone

cards.q: Apply the rhetorical situation to a photograph or political cartoon.
cards.a: Treat the image as an argument: identify its maker (writer), the viewers it targets (audience), what prompted it (exigence), when and where it appeared (context), what it claims (message), and what it wants viewers to think or do (purpose). Then read framing, caption, labels, symbols, exaggeration, and juxtaposition as choices serving that purpose.
cards.h: → six components, then visual choices as rhetoric
cards.n: In the synthesis essay, a chart or cartoon cited as decoration earns nothing; say what it argues and how its design serves that argument.

cards.q: Define the choice-effect-purpose chain in rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: It is the unit of commentary: name a specific rhetorical choice, explain its effect on the intended audience, then connect that effect to the writer's purpose in this situation. It turns the enduring understanding (writers make strategic choices based on their situation) into a sentence a reader can score.
cards.n: Commentary that stops at the effect ('this creates emotion') floats; the link to purpose and audience is what Row B rewards.

cards.q: Identify the six components of the rhetorical situation in this headnote: 'In October, after a wildfire destroyed the only public library in a mountain town, a retired schoolteacher who had volunteered there for thirty years wrote a letter to the county newspaper urging residents to approve a bond measure on the November ballot to rebuild it. She argues that the library was the town's only free indoor public space.'
cards.a: Exigence: the fire that destroyed the library, with a bond vote weeks away. Purpose: to persuade residents to vote yes. Audience: county newspaper readers who vote, including people who never used the library. Writer: a retired teacher and thirty-year volunteer. Context: a small town after a fire, before an election. Message: the library was the town's only free indoor public space and must be rebuilt.
cards.n: Naming 'the library' as the exigence confuses subject with trigger: the exigence is the fire plus the coming vote.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical triangle.
cards.a: The model showing the three interlocking elements of any rhetorical act: the speaker (ethos), the audience (pathos), and the subject or message (logos). A change in one reshapes the others.
cards.n: The triangle maps appeals onto positions: ethos lives with the speaker, pathos with the audience, logos with the subject.

cards.q: Explain why a rhetorical analysis should read the passage's headnote before the passage itself.
cards.a: The headnote supplies the writer, audience, occasion, and date, the components that make choices explainable. Knowing that a speaker is a surgeon addressing new nurses lets commentary say why her anecdote about a night shift persuades them, rather than only noting that she tells a story.
cards.h: → headnote names writer, audience, context → choices can be tied to them → commentary instead of summary
cards.n: 'The headnote gives background' is too vague; say which components it supplies and which choice they help explain.
o: The headnote is the exam's shortcut to the rhetorical situation, so skipping it forces the essay to guess at audience and purpose.
Row B commentary must explain how choices work for a specific audience, and the headnote is where that audience is named.

w.a: The headnote is important because it gives background information about the passage.
w.why: vague; never says which components it supplies or how they serve analysis

w.a: You should read the headnote so you can summarize the speaker's life in your introduction.
w.why: biography is summary, not analysis of choices

w.a: The headnote tells you which rhetorical devices the writer is going to use.
w.why: false; it gives the situation, not the devices

cards.q: Explain why the same sentence can be effective in one rhetorical situation and ineffective in another.
cards.a: Effectiveness is measured against a purpose and an audience, not in the abstract. A blunt statistic can persuade a budget committee that needs numbers yet feel cold at a memorial, where the audience needs its loss acknowledged; the sentence is the same, the situation is not.
cards.h: → effect depends on purpose, audience, context → change the situation → change the effect
cards.n: Judging a sentence 'good writing' in the abstract earns nothing; effectiveness is always relative to this audience and purpose.
o: Because writers choose with a particular exigence and audience in mind, a choice is a good one only relative to those conditions.
Audiences bring different beliefs, values, and needs, so the same words meet different expectations in different settings.

w.a: Some sentences are simply better written than others, no matter where they appear.
w.why: ignores that the rhetorical situation defines effectiveness

w.a: A sentence is effective whenever it uses strong rhetorical devices.
w.why: devices have no effect independent of purpose and audience

cards.q: Explain why a writer's identity can change how an audience receives the same message.
cards.a: The writer is one component of the situation: who speaks shapes what the audience assumes about motive and expertise. A plea for safer crosswalks from a parent whose child was struck carries lived authority; the same words from a paving contractor invite suspicion of profit, so the audience weighs them differently.
cards.h: → writer's identity → audience infers motive and expertise → credibility → acceptance
cards.n: Saying 'the writer is credible' without naming the trait and the audience's inference is a label, not an explanation.
o: Audiences judge a message partly by its source, so a writer's experience, stake, or role can lend or cost credibility.
The writer's relationship to the audience, insider or outsider, sets how much trust the message starts with.

w.a: The identity of the writer does not matter because a good argument stands on its own.
w.why: ignores that audiences weigh credibility and motive

w.a: A famous writer is always more persuasive than an unknown one.
w.why: overgeneralizes; fit to this audience, not fame, matters

cards.q: Define exigence.
cards.a: The exigence is the part of a rhetorical situation that inspires, stimulates, provokes, or prompts a writer to create a text: a specific event, problem, or condition, such as a new policy, a crisis, or a published attack, that makes the writer respond now.
cards.n: Exigence is the trigger, not the topic: 'education' is a subject; 'the board's vote to cut the arts budget' is an exigence.
x: the reason the text was written
what prompts the writer to write

cards.q: Contrast exigence and occasion.
cards.a: The exigence is what prompts the text (a problem, event, or condition demanding a response); the occasion is the specific event, time, and place where the text is delivered, part of its context. A town's grief and anger after a factory fire is the exigence; the memorial service where the mayor speaks is the occasion.
cards.n: Students collapse these; on an MC question asking for the exigence, the choice naming the ceremony or venue is usually the trap.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to apologize (atone).
cards.a: To acknowledge a wrong, accept responsibility, and express regret in order to repair damaged trust. It is the purpose most directly dictated by its exigence, a specific harm the writer caused, which the apology must name precisely for the audience to accept it.
cards.n: A 'mistakes were made' apology hedges responsibility; analysis asks whether the apology's choices answer the specific harm that prompted it.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to justify.
cards.a: To give reasons or evidence that make a past or proposed action appear reasonable, necessary, or fair. Its exigence is usually a challenge (criticism, an investigation, a controversial decision), so the text defends a decision already made rather than winning readers to a new position.
cards.h: → definition + the exigence that calls for it
cards.n: Calling a justification simply 'persuasive' is too loose; name what was challenged and how the reasons answer that challenge.
x: give reasons an action was fair

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to warn.
cards.a: To alert an audience to a danger or likely consequence so that they change course before it arrives. Its exigence is a threat the writer perceives as near and preventable (a flood forecast, a budget shortfall), which is why warnings stress time and consequence.
cards.n: A warning with no preventable outcome is only lament; say what the audience can still do and why the writer thinks the time is now.

cards.q: Identify the exigence of this passage and the words that signal it: 'Last Tuesday, for the third time since March, the Elm Street bridge flooded and a school bus carrying twenty-two children had to turn back through rising water. I am writing to the county commission because the repair it postponed in January can no longer wait.' (a parent's letter to the county commission)
cards.a: The exigence is the third flooding of the Elm Street bridge last Tuesday, which forced a bus of children to turn back, after the commission had postponed the repair. 'Last Tuesday, for the third time since March' marks the prompting event; 'can no longer wait' marks the urgency that makes the parent write now.
cards.n: Answering 'bridge safety' names the subject, not the exigence; the answer must name the specific event that prompted this letter.

cards.q:
Identify the most likely exigence of each text:
1. A principal's letter to parents two days after a student's allergic reaction in the cafeteria
2. An op-ed titled 'Keep the Pool Open,' published the week the parks board posts its budget cuts
3. A graduation speech to nursing students in a year of severe hospital staffing shortages
4. A company statement issued the morning after its app exposed customers' home addresses
5. A scientist's letter to a newspaper after a viral post misreported her study
6. A eulogy for a town's mail carrier of forty years
7. A student editorial after the district eliminated the late bus
8. A mayor's radio address the morning after a flood
9. A coach's email to players after the team's third forfeit for low attendance
10. A petition circulated the day after a popular teacher's contract was not renewed
cards.a:
1 → the allergic reaction, which made parents fear for their children's safety at lunch
2 → the proposed cut that threatens to close the pool
3 → the staffing shortage the graduates are about to enter (the ceremony is only the occasion)
4 → the exposure of customer data and the loss of trust it caused
5 → the misreporting of her findings spreading online
6 → the carrier's death and the town's grief
7 → the elimination of the late bus
8 → the flood's damage and residents' fear and need for information
9 → the third forfeit caused by low attendance
10 → the non-renewal of the teacher's contract
cards.n: For item 3, 'graduation' is the occasion, not the exigence; the exigence is the condition that makes this speech's message necessary.

cards.q: Identify the best description of the writer's exigence: 'When the council voted last night to sell Harmon Field to a developer, it did so without a single public hearing. Families who have played there for sixty years learned of the sale from a sign on the fence this morning.' (A) The rising cost of housing in the city (B) The council's sale of Harmon Field without public input (C) The history of youth sports in the city (D) A sign posted on the fence this morning
cards.a: (B). The prompting event is the council's vote to sell the field without a hearing; the passage opens with it, and every detail (sixty years, a sign on the fence) sharpens its unfairness. (A) is a context the passage never names, (C) is background, and (D) is how families learned of the sale, a detail rather than the cause of writing.
cards.n: Exigence distractors often name a real detail from the passage; the exigence is the event that makes the text necessary, not any fact it mentions.

cards.q: Apply SOAPSTone: explain why it has no separate letter for exigence.
cards.a: SOAPSTone folds the prompting event into Occasion, so it blurs the trigger with the setting. The CED separates them: exigence is what provokes the text, while occasion is part of its context. A reader using SOAPSTone must add exigence deliberately, since the exam asks for it directly.
cards.h: → acronym merges trigger into Occasion → CED separates exigence from context → add it yourself
cards.n: SOAPSTone is a classroom mnemonic, not CED language; the CED's first sample multiple-choice question asks for the writer's exigence.
o: The acronym tracks what is visible on the surface (speaker, occasion, subject), while exigence often has to be inferred from why the text appeared when it did.
Its Occasion slot is meant to cover both the event and the setting, which hides the difference between what prompted the text and where it was delivered.

w.a: SOAPSTone has no letter for exigence because exigence is the same thing as the subject.
w.why: confuses the trigger with the topic

w.a: Exigence does not matter much for analysis, so SOAPSTone leaves it out.
w.why: false; exigence explains why the text and its choices exist

cards.q: Explain why a writer responding to a crisis often names the prompting event in the first sentence.
cards.a: Naming the event states the exigence the audience already feels, so the text's relevance is immediate and the writer shows awareness of what readers are living through. It also makes the call to act timely: the sooner the event is on the page, the sooner the demand seems urgent rather than abstract.
cards.h: → name the event → shared exigence → relevance + urgency → the audience keeps reading
cards.n: 'To grab the reader's attention' is generic; say what naming this event does for an audience already shaken by it.
o: Opening on the event proves the writer is responding to the audience's situation, not delivering a prepared lecture.
Stating the exigence first frames everything that follows as a response to it, so the audience reads each claim as part of a solution.

w.a: Writers name the event first because every essay should start with a hook.
w.why: a formula, not a reason tied to exigence and audience

w.a: Naming the event first is just a way to summarize what happened.
w.why: misses the effect on the audience and the purpose

cards.q: Explain why 'climate change' is a weak answer to the question 'What is this op-ed's exigence?'
cards.a: It names a broad subject, not the specific event that prompted this text. An exigence explains why the writer wrote now: a heat wave that closed schools, a vote to repeal a regulation. Only a specific trigger lets analysis connect the writer's choices to what the audience is reacting to.
cards.h: → subject ≠ trigger → exigence must be specific → only a trigger explains the choices
cards.n: Any answer that could describe a thousand texts on the same subject has not found this text's exigence.
o: The exigence is time-bound and particular, while a subject like climate change could prompt texts in any year.
Analysis needs the trigger because choices such as urgency or a call to act respond to that event, not to the subject in general.

w.a: Climate change is the exigence because it is the main topic of the op-ed.
w.why: equates the topic with the prompting event

w.a: Any major issue in the news counts as an exigence for an op-ed.
w.why: too broad to explain any specific choice

cards.q: Define purpose in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The purpose of a text is what the writer hopes to accomplish with it, and a writer may have more than one purpose in a text. State it as a verb aimed at the audience: to persuade voters to reject the bond, to reassure parents, to shame a board into acting.
cards.h: → CED definition + purpose stated as a verb
cards.n: 'To use rhetorical devices' or 'to inform people about the topic' is not a purpose; name what the writer wants this audience to think, feel, or do.
x: what the writer hopes to accomplish

cards.q: Contrast purpose and message.
cards.a: The message is what the text says, its central claim; the purpose is what the writer wants that message to do to the audience. 'Public libraries are democracy's classrooms' is a message; to persuade council members to restore library funding is the purpose the message serves.
cards.n: A thesis that only restates the message ('she says libraries matter') summarizes; one naming the purpose and the choices that serve it analyzes.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to critique.
cards.a: To evaluate a subject by exposing its flaws or limits against a standard, stated or implied, that the subject fails to meet. A critique judges rather than merely describes, and its audience must accept the standard for the judgment to land.
cards.n: Name the standard the writer measures by; 'she criticizes the policy' leaves out what makes the critique persuasive to this audience.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to satirize.
cards.a: To ridicule a person, institution, or practice through irony, exaggeration, or mockery in order to expose folly or vice and imply the need for reform. The speaker's surface proposal differs from the author's real purpose, the critique the absurdity exposes.
cards.n: Borrows irony from Style: satire has a corrective target; if you cannot name what the author wants changed, you have not found the purpose.

cards.q: Apply the correct purpose verb: a senator recounts a factory closure, then urges passage of a retraining bill.
cards.a: Two purposes, one serving the other: to move the audience by making the closure a human loss, and ultimately to persuade them to support the retraining bill. The anecdote serves the persuasive purpose by turning an abstract policy into consequences for real workers, which the call to pass the bill then answers.
cards.h: → primary + secondary purpose, then how they connect
cards.n: Naming only 'to inform' misses the call to act; a text may have more than one purpose, and the strongest answer ranks them.

cards.q: Contrast a text's stated purpose and its functional purpose.
cards.a: The stated purpose is what a text claims to be doing, such as 'simply presenting the facts'; the functional purpose is what its choices actually accomplish, such as persuading through selected facts and loaded words. Analysis tests the claim against the choices.
cards.h: → claimed aim vs what the choices do
cards.n: A text that announces neutrality while loading its diction is a classic analysis target; quote the loaded words as evidence of the functional purpose.

cards.q: Decide the purpose: a CEO's memo after a data breach names exactly what happened, states who is responsible, and outlines concrete remedies.
cards.a: The dominant purpose is to restore trust by accepting responsibility (an apology in substance), with secondary purposes to inform readers of what happened and to reassure them that remedies are under way. Naming the failure precisely and listing remedies serve all three, since vague language would read as evasion.
cards.n: Real texts blend purposes; name the dominant one and the secondary ones, then show which choice serves which.

cards.q: Identify the writer's purposes in this passage: 'Our doors will close for renovation on June 1. We know this is hard news for the families who visit every Saturday, and we are sorry for the long wait. But the new wing will double the space for children's exhibits, and every gift made this month will be matched by the Harlow Foundation.' (a museum director's letter to members)
cards.a: Three purposes: to inform members of the closure date; to console or apologize to regular families ('we are sorry for the long wait'); and, dominantly, to persuade members to donate, which the 'But' pivot, the promised benefit, and the matching gift serve. The apology comes first so readers are receptive before the request.
cards.h: → each purpose + the words that serve it
cards.n: Stopping at 'to inform' misses the pivot at 'But'; the EK's point is that a text may carry several purposes, one usually dominant.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to persuade.
cards.a: To move an audience to accept a claim, adopt an attitude, or take a specific action by giving them reasons and motives to do so.
cards.n: Persuade is the default guess and the weakest answer; a sharper verb such as warn, unify or mobilize almost always scores better.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to inform.
cards.a: To convey facts or explain a subject clearly to an audience without primarily arguing a contested position, though the selection of facts can still carry a slant worth noticing.
cards.n: Calling a text purely informative is a common misread, so check what the writer chose to leave out before settling on that label.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to inspire.
cards.a: To move an audience toward hope, ambition, or renewed commitment by appealing to shared ideals rather than by presenting new evidence or arguing a contested claim.
cards.n: Inspire and persuade differ in what they ask for: inspire seeks a change in feeling and commitment, persuade a change in position.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to mobilize.
cards.a: To move an audience from agreement to action, giving them a specific, immediate step to take rather than simply changing what they believe.
cards.n: Mobilize goes further than persuade - the audience may already agree; the text asks them to act now.
x: move an audience to act now

cards.q: Explain why a rhetorical analysis thesis must name the writer's purpose, not just restate the topic.
cards.a: Row A rewards a thesis that analyzes the writer's choices, and choices can only be analyzed as means to an end. Naming the purpose (to persuade graduates to take risks) gives the essay a defensible claim and gives each body paragraph a job: showing how a choice serves that purpose.
cards.h: → choices are means to an end → name the end → a defensible claim + a job for each paragraph
cards.n: A device-list thesis fails the same way: it names the tools the writer reached for without naming the goal those tools serve.
o: A topic ('this speech is about perseverance') restates the prompt, which the rubric says earns no thesis point.
Without a purpose, commentary cannot explain why a choice works, so the essay slides into listing devices.

w.a: The thesis should list three devices the writer uses so the reader knows what paragraphs are coming.
w.why: a device list without a purpose is not analysis of choices

w.a: The writer uses many rhetorical strategies to convey her message to the audience.
w.why: restates the prompt, which earns no thesis point

w.a: Naming the purpose is optional as long as the thesis mentions the audience.
w.why: audience without purpose leaves the choices unexplained

cards.q: Explain why stating a purpose with a precise verb ('to shame the board into acting') makes better commentary than 'to persuade.'
cards.a: Nearly every argument aims to persuade, so the general verb explains no particular choice. A precise verb names the effect sought on this audience, which lets commentary show why a specific choice fits: public shame explains why the writer lists the board's broken promises by date.
cards.h: → 'persuade' fits everything → precise verb names the intended effect → choices can be matched to it
cards.n: 'The purpose is to persuade the audience' is true of almost every passage, so it cannot explain why this writer made this choice.
o: A precise purpose verb turns commentary into cause and effect: this choice produces this reaction, which advances this aim.
Readers score commentary that ties a choice to purpose; a vague purpose gives the choice nothing specific to tie to.

w.a: It does not matter which verb you use as long as you mention the purpose once.
w.why: a vague purpose cannot explain specific choices

w.a: 'To persuade' is always the best purpose because arguments persuade.
w.why: true of everything, so it explains nothing

cards.q: Explain why a writer might pursue two purposes at once, such as consoling and calling to action.
cards.a: Audiences often need one thing before they can accept another. Grieving listeners must feel their loss acknowledged before a call to act seems respectful, so the consoling purpose earns the hearing that the persuasive purpose then uses; the first purpose prepares the audience for the second.
cards.h: → audience's immediate need → first purpose meets it → trust → second purpose lands
cards.n: Treating two purposes as the writer being 'unfocused' misreads the text; say how one purpose prepares the audience for the other.
o: Mixed audiences may need different things, so one purpose can serve some listeners while the other serves the rest.
A secondary purpose can remove an obstacle (grief, anger, confusion) that would otherwise block the primary one.

w.a: Writers use two purposes so the essay will be longer and more detailed.
w.why: no link to the audience's needs

w.a: A good writer should only ever have one purpose in a text.
w.why: contradicts the EK, which says writers may have more than one

cards.q: Define audience in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The audience is the readers or listeners a writer intends to reach. In the CED's words, an audience has shared as well as individual beliefs, values, needs, and backgrounds, so describe an audience by what it believes, values, and needs, not only by who is present.
cards.n: 'The audience is the people listening' earns nothing; name what they believe, value, or need that the writer's choices address.

cards.q: Contrast primary and secondary audience.
cards.a: The primary audience is the group the writer directly addresses and most wants to move; the secondary audience is anyone else who will receive the text, such as the press, opponents, or later readers. The two may hold different beliefs and needs, so a choice aimed at one can be read differently by the other.
cards.n: Public speeches often argue past the room: the graduates are primary, the parents and press secondary; say which audience a choice is aimed at.

cards.q: Explain what is meant by audience assumptions.
cards.a: Audience assumptions are the beliefs, knowledge, and attitudes a writer takes for granted that the audience already holds, so the text builds on them without arguing for them. They are the shared beliefs and values the EK describes, and a writer who misjudges them leaves the argument resting on ground the audience does not accept.
cards.n: Naming an unstated assumption and showing the argument depends on it is a strong Row B move, and sometimes a Row C one.

cards.q: Identify King's stated audience in Letter from Birmingham Jail based on its opening line, and note who else was really listening.
cards.a: The stated audience is the eight white Alabama clergymen who had published a statement calling his demonstrations 'unwise and untimely'; 'My Dear Fellow Clergymen' addresses them as peers. King wrote knowing a far wider public, including white moderates across the nation, would read the letter, so his choices answer both.
cards.n: Writing to a named audience while expecting a wider one is itself a choice; say which audience a given passage of the letter is aimed at.

cards.q: Define the invoked audience in rhetoric.
cards.a: The invoked audience is the audience a text constructs within itself through its assumptions, address, and references ('fellow parents,' 'those of us who remember the old mill'), whether or not every actual reader fits that profile. Invoking an audience invites readers to adopt the beliefs and values attributed to it.
cards.n: Not a CED term and never asked by name; use it to explain how a writer invites readers into shared values.

cards.q: Contrast the invoked audience and the actual audience of a text.
cards.a: The invoked audience is whom the text's language and assumptions address, such as 'concerned parents'; the actual audience is whoever really reads or hears it, which may be broader and hold individual beliefs the invoked profile ignores. The gap explains why a text can unite some readers and alienate others.
cards.n: A published letter can invoke one small audience while being read by everyone; check whose beliefs each choice assumes.

cards.q: Define the universal audience as a rhetorical concept.
cards.a: An imagined audience of all reasonable people, used as a standard: an argument aimed at it relies on reasoning any thoughtful reader would accept rather than on the particular beliefs of one group. It sits at the opposite end from an audience defined by individual beliefs and backgrounds.
cards.n: Not a CED term; use it to judge whether an appeal persuades broadly or plays only to one group's shared assumptions.

cards.q: Identify one belief the audience likely shares and two individual differences the writer must anticipate: a school board member will speak to a meeting of parents about replacing paper textbooks with tablets next fall.
cards.a: Shared: the parents want their children to learn well and to have fair access to materials. Individual differences: some families lack reliable home internet, so tablets could widen gaps; some parents worry about screen time; some focus on cost as taxpayers. The speaker must honor the shared value while answering each concern.
cards.h: → one shared value + two individual differences
cards.n: Describing the audience as 'parents' is demographics; the EK asks for beliefs, values, needs, and backgrounds, shared and individual.

cards.q: Explain why describing an audience only by demographics ('adults in 1963') weakens a rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: Choices work on what an audience believes, values, and needs, not on age or date. 'Adults in 1963' cannot explain why an appeal to religious duty would move them; 'churchgoing moderates who value order' can, so commentary needs the audience's beliefs to connect a choice to its effect.
cards.h: → choices act on beliefs and values → demographics name neither → commentary cannot link choice to effect
cards.n: Rubrics reward understanding of the rhetorical situation; a census description of the audience shows none.
o: The EK defines audience by beliefs, values, needs, and backgrounds, so an analysis that omits them has not described the audience.
Two audiences of the same age can hold opposite values, so demographics cannot predict how a choice will land.

w.a: Describing the audience's age and location is enough to show you understand it.
w.why: names who, not what they believe or need

w.a: The audience does not matter much in rhetorical analysis; the devices matter.
w.why: devices have effects only on a particular audience

cards.q: Explain why a writer addressing a divided audience often appeals first to a value the whole audience shares.
cards.a: A shared value (children's safety, fairness) is ground no listener will dispute, so it earns a hearing from both sides before the contested claim. Starting there frames the claim as an application of what everyone already believes, which lowers the resistance of those who disagree.
cards.h: → shared value → no one objects → both sides keep listening → claim framed as following from it
cards.n: 'To connect with the audience' is too vague; name the shared value and why it matters that the whole audience holds it.
o: Opening on common values shows the writer sees the audience as one community, not as allies and enemies.
Disagreement usually concerns means, not ends, so beginning with the shared end narrows the dispute.

w.a: Writers start with shared values because it is polite to agree with people.
w.why: politeness is not the rhetorical effect

w.a: Appealing to shared values means the writer has no real argument.
w.why: the shared value is the premise the argument builds on

cards.q: Explain why a writer addressing an audience with individual differences might acknowledge those differences openly.
cards.a: Naming differences ('some of you drive an hour to work, some of you walk') shows the writer sees each reader's situation, which builds goodwill. It also keeps readers whose needs differ from the majority's from feeling ignored and dismissing the argument as not meant for them.
cards.h: → name the differences → readers feel seen → goodwill + no one opts out
cards.n: Claiming the writer 'relates to everyone' misses the mechanism: specific acknowledgment of individual needs.
o: Acknowledging differences lets the writer answer each group's likely objection before it forms.
An audience that feels its variety is recognized is more willing to accept a common solution.

w.a: Acknowledging differences weakens an argument by showing the audience is divided.
w.why: ignores the goodwill it builds

w.a: Writers mention differences to show off how much they know about the audience.
w.why: no link to acceptance or purpose

cards.q: Define context in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: Context is the set of circumstances in which a writer creates a text, which the CED says includes the time, place, and occasion. It also takes in the historical, cultural, and political conditions of that moment, which shape what the audience already knows and expects, and so which choices will work.
