cards.a: Connotation is the emotional, cultural, and evaluative association a word carries beyond its literal meaning, e.g. 'thrifty,' 'frugal,' and 'stingy' all denote careful with money but connote praise, neutrality, and blame. Connotation lets a writer's bias show through apparently neutral description, which affects credibility with readers who notice it.
cards.n: Borrows connotation from Style; for RHS credit, tie the connotation to the writer's bias and to how this audience will judge it.

cards.q: Define euphemism and give an example.
cards.a: A mild or indirect expression substituted for a harsh or blunt one, e.g. 'downsizing' for firing workers, 'collateral damage' for civilian deaths. It can show tact toward a grieving audience, but when it hides responsibility, readers who see through it judge the writer evasive and credibility falls.
cards.n: Ask what the softer word protects the audience from noticing, and whether this audience will accept or resent the softening.

cards.q: Define bias as it applies to a source or speaker.
cards.a: Bias is a predisposition, interest, or perspective that shapes what a writer notices, includes, and omits. Word choice may reveal it, and a writer whose bias shows through unfair or one-sided language may lose credibility with an audience that does not share it.
cards.h: → definition + how word choice reveals it
cards.n: In synthesis, naming a source's stake and how it shapes its evidence is stronger than dismissing the source as 'biased.'

cards.q: Contrast ethos and credibility.
cards.a: Ethos is the appeal to the writer's character and authority; credibility is the trustworthiness an audience actually grants. A writer can attempt ethos (list credentials) and still lose credibility with an audience if the word choice seems biased, condescending, or careless.
cards.n: Credibility is earned or lost in the text, word by word, with a particular audience; ethos names the kind of appeal.

cards.q: Identify the textual markers that signal a writer is building credibility.
cards.a: First-person experience with the subject, credentials named or implied, precise and fairly cited evidence, measured and qualified language, fair summaries of opponents, and vocabulary or values shared with the audience. Each is a word-level choice an audience reads as a sign of an unbiased, trustworthy writer.
cards.n: Spotting a marker is identification; commentary must say why this audience would trust the writer more because of it.

cards.q: Analyze how the word choice affects the writer's credibility with undecided readers: 'The so-called developers have cooked up yet another scheme to bulldoze the wetlands, and their paid cheerleaders on the council are already lining up to rubber-stamp it.' (a letter to a town newspaper before a zoning vote)
cards.a: Loaded words ('so-called,' 'cooked up,' 'scheme,' 'bulldoze,' 'paid cheerleaders,' 'rubber-stamp') reveal the writer's bias against the project and imply corruption without evidence. Readers who already oppose it may cheer, but undecided readers are likely to see the writer as unfair and discount the letter's real concern about the wetlands.
cards.h: → loaded words + bias revealed + effect on this audience
cards.n: 'The writer uses loaded language' is identification only; the EK asks how the words affect credibility with a particular audience.

cards.q: Write a revision of this sentence that keeps its position but would preserve credibility with readers who support the project: 'The greedy developers want to destroy our wetlands for a quick buck.'
cards.a: Model: 'The development would fill twelve acres of wetland that absorb floodwater for the east side, a cost the proposal's projected tax revenue does not account for.' It keeps the opposition but replaces motive-attacking words ('greedy,' 'quick buck') with a specific, checkable consequence, so supporters must answer the argument instead of dismissing the writer.
cards.h: → one revised sentence + what changed and why
cards.n: Merely deleting 'greedy' leaves no argument; the revision needs specific, neutral language that carries the claim.

cards.q: Explain why a writer who uses neutral language about opponents often gains credibility with undecided readers.
cards.a: Undecided readers watch how a writer treats the other side as a test of fairness. Neutral language shows the writer is not driven by bias, so readers trust the writer's facts and judgment; name-calling signals that the conclusion came before the evidence.
cards.h: → undecided readers test fairness → neutral words pass the test → facts trusted → claim considered
cards.n: 'Neutral language is more polite' misses the mechanism: fairness toward opponents is evidence the writer's judgment can be trusted.
o: Fair wording lets undecided readers imagine agreeing without joining a side that insults people they know.
Loaded words give opponents an easy reason to dismiss the whole argument, which neutral wording denies them.

w.a: Writers should use neutral language so they do not hurt anyone's feelings.
w.why: politeness, not credibility

w.a: Neutral language is weaker because it shows the writer does not care.
w.why: confuses restraint with indifference

cards.q: Explain why the same loaded word can strengthen a writer's credibility with one audience and weaken it with another.
cards.a: A loaded word signals whose side the writer is on. Readers who share that bias hear it as honest conviction and trust the writer more; readers who do not hear it as prejudice and trust the writer less. As the EK says, credibility depends on the particular audience.
cards.h: → loaded word shows the writer's side → allies hear conviction → others hear bias → credibility splits
cards.n: Judging a word 'good' or 'bad' in the abstract ignores the EK's phrase 'with a particular audience.'
o: Word choice is read through the audience's own values, so the same connotation lands as insight or insult.
A rally audience rewards shared language as loyalty, while a mixed audience punishes it as partisanship.

w.a: Loaded words always damage a writer's credibility.
w.why: ignores audiences who share the bias

w.a: Loaded words are persuasive because they are emotional.
w.why: names pathos without the audience-dependent effect

cards.q: Explain why a euphemism in a corporate apology can cost the company credibility.
cards.a: An apology's audience wants the harm named plainly. Calling layoffs 'a realignment of resources' signals that the company is shielding itself, so readers perceive the apology as evasive and doubt its promises; blunt words would show the accountability the audience demands.
cards.h: → audience wants the harm named → euphemism shields the company → apology seems evasive → promises doubted
cards.n: 'Euphemisms are vague' is true but thin; say what this audience needs from an apology and how the softening denies it.
o: The euphemism reveals a bias toward protecting the company, which contradicts the apology's stated purpose.
Readers who were harmed recognize the softened term as spin, and spin is the opposite of the candor an apology promises.

w.a: Euphemisms make an apology sound more professional.
w.why: ignores the audience's need for accountability

w.a: The company used a euphemism so the apology would be shorter.
w.why: no link to credibility or audience

cards.q: Define a straw man rebuttal and explain why it damages ethos even when it wins the exchange.
cards.a: A straw man rebuttal attacks a weakened or distorted version of the opposing view instead of the view itself. Even when it seems to win, readers who hold or know the real position see the misrepresentation as unfair and biased, so the writer loses credibility with exactly the audience the argument needed to move.
cards.h: → distort the opposing view → easy win → informed readers see unfairness → credibility lost where it mattered
cards.n: Borrows refutation from Claims and Evidence; 'it is a logical fallacy' names the flaw but not its cost with this audience.
o: Undecided readers judge a writer's fairness by how accurately the other side is summarized, so a caricature signals bias.
Readers who hold the opposing view hear it misstated, conclude the writer never understood it, and stop listening.

w.a: A straw man is effective because it makes the other side look weak.
w.why: ignores how informed readers judge the distortion

w.a: A straw man only hurts the writer if the opponent points it out.
w.why: readers can recognize the distortion themselves

cards.q: Apply audience analysis: a price-hike memo will reach both loyal customers and industry regulators. What adjustment does this demand?
cards.a: The writer must adapt one text for two audiences with different perspectives and needs: loyal customers need reassurance and a sense of continued value, conveyed through tone and plain language, while regulators need factual justification, costs, and compliance detail. Evidence, organization, and language must serve both without contradicting either.
cards.h: → each audience's need + the adjustment it demands
cards.n: With a mixed audience no single appeal can carry the whole text; name which part addresses which audience's need.

cards.q: Define a captive audience and explain how it changes rhetorical strategy.
cards.a: An audience that must receive a message regardless of interest, such as students at a mandatory assembly. Because their attention is not self-selected, the writer must earn engagement by choosing evidence, examples, and language drawn from their perspective rather than assuming interest.
cards.n: A captive audience is not automatically hostile, only not self-selected; the needed adjustment is engagement, not concession.

cards.q: Define jargon and give an example.
cards.a: Specialized vocabulary of a profession or field, e.g. 'amortization,' 'titrate,' 'tort.' With specialists it signals expertise and saves time; with a general audience it excludes and confuses, so a writer considering the audience's context must define it or replace it.
cards.n: Borrows the term from Style; jargon is never good or bad in itself, only fitted or unfitted to this audience's background.

cards.q: Define colloquial diction and give an example.
cards.a: Informal, conversational word choice from everyday speech, e.g. 'kind of a mess,' 'no big deal,' 'y'all.' With a peer audience it closes distance and signals sincerity or shared identity; with a formal audience, such as a hearing board, it can cost the writer authority.
cards.n: Borrows from Style; judge colloquial language by the audience's context and expectations, not by a rule that informal is wrong.

cards.q: Define appeal to authority.
cards.a: Support drawn from the testimony of an expert, institution, or respected figure, borrowing that source's credibility for the writer's claim. It persuades only when the audience recognizes and respects the authority, so writers choose authorities from the audience's own perspective (a coach for athletes, a pediatrician for parents).
cards.n: Borrows expert opinion as evidence from Claims and Evidence; an authority this audience distrusts, or one irrelevant to the claim, adds nothing.

cards.q: Identify how the writer changed evidence, organization, and language for each audience. Version 1, to the city council: 'Adding a crossing guard at Fifth and Main would cost 14,000 dollars a year; the intersection saw nine pedestrian injuries last year, and the city's liability for one serious injury exceeds 200,000 dollars.' Version 2, to parents in a school newsletter: 'Last spring, a second-grader was clipped by a turning truck at Fifth and Main. A crossing guard there would mean one more adult watching for our kids. Come to Tuesday's council meeting.'
cards.a: Evidence: the council gets cost, injury counts, and liability, matching its budget perspective; parents get one child's near miss, matching their fear. Organization: the council version reasons from cost to benefit; the parent version moves from story to image to a call to act. Language: impersonal and numerical for officials, personal ('our kids') for parents.
cards.h: → evidence, organization, language, one line each
cards.n: Noticing only that 'one version is more emotional' misses two of the EK's three levers: evidence and organization change too.

cards.q: Decide which evidence would best persuade an audience of rural county commissioners to fund a mobile health clinic. (A) A national report on the rising cost of urban emergency rooms (B) A statement from a celebrity health advocate (C) The county's own data showing residents drive an average of 48 miles to the nearest clinic, and a neighboring county's figures after its mobile clinic cut ambulance calls by a fifth (D) A description of a hospital's new surgical wing
cards.a: (C). It uses the commissioners' own county data and a comparable rural county's result, evidence drawn from their context that answers their need to justify spending. (A) addresses cities, not their county; (B) relies on an authority they have no reason to trust on local needs; (D) is irrelevant to a mobile clinic.
cards.h: → letter + fit to the audience's context + why others fail
cards.n: The trap is the most impressive-sounding source; the exam rewards evidence drawn from this audience's perspective and needs.

cards.q: Write the same claim, that the town should build a dog park, twice: once for the parks budget committee and once for dog owners in a neighborhood newsletter.
cards.a: Committee: 'A fenced dog park on the unused lot at Birch Road would be a one-time capital cost and would reduce the off-leash complaints that now take up much of park staff's time.' Newsletter: 'Imagine a place where your dog can run full speed off the leash, and you can stop apologizing to joggers. Help us build it at Birch Road.' Each matches its audience's needs: cost versus daily life.
cards.h: → two versions + the need each serves
cards.n: Writing the same sentence with different adjectives misses the EK: evidence and organization, not just words, must change with the audience.

cards.q: Explain how a writer adapts diction for a specialist audience versus a general audience.
cards.a: For specialists, the writer uses technical terms undefined and skips steps, which signals competence and respects their time. For a general audience, the writer defines or replaces jargon and spells out the reasoning, because the audience's background, not the subject, sets how much must be explained.
cards.h: → audience background sets the level → specialists: terms + skipped steps → general: definitions + explained steps
cards.n: Borrows diction from Style; overexplaining to experts is as much a misstep as underexplaining to a general reader.
o: The same content needs different language because audiences differ in the contexts and needs they bring.
Undefined jargon tells a general reader the text is not for them, while defined terms invite them in.

w.a: A writer should always use simple words so that everyone can understand.
w.why: ignores that specialists expect precision

w.a: Using technical terms always makes the writer more credible.
w.why: true only with an audience that shares them

cards.q: Explain why an appeal can backfire with a particular audience.
cards.a: An appeal backfires when it assumes beliefs, knowledge, or trust the audience lacks. Heavy pathos can feel manipulative to a skeptical audience, and dense data can alienate a general one; because audiences are unique, an appeal that moves one group can harden another against the writer.
cards.h: → appeal assumes what the audience lacks → mismatch → reader resists → writer's position weakens
cards.n: Judging fit to audience, not just naming the appeal, separates analysis from labeling.
o: The same appeal meets different perspectives, contexts, and needs, so its effect depends on who receives it.
An appeal that feels like pressure to the wrong audience reveals the writer's misreading of them, which costs credibility.

w.a: Appeals only backfire when the writer uses them incorrectly.
w.why: ignores that fit depends on the audience

w.a: Pathos always backfires because emotional arguments are weak.
w.why: overgeneralizes about one appeal

cards.q: Explain why a writer speaking to the same audience a second time, after a failed vote, should change the argument.
cards.a: Audiences are dynamic: after the vote they know the first argument and have already rejected it. Repeating it invites the same result, so the writer must address the reasons they voted no (cost, trust), perhaps with new evidence or a revised proposal, meeting the audience where it now stands.
cards.h: → audience changed by the vote → old argument already rejected → answer their reasons → new evidence
cards.n: 'Try harder' or 'say it louder' ignores the EK's word 'dynamic': the audience's perspective has moved since the first argument.
o: The vote revealed the audience's real objections, so the writer now knows which needs the second argument must meet.
An unchanged argument signals the writer did not listen, which costs goodwill with an audience that has already said no.

w.a: The writer should repeat the same argument because persistence eventually wins.
w.why: ignores the audience's changed perspective

w.a: The writer should find a completely different audience instead.
w.why: evades the task of adapting to this audience

cards.q: Define a claim in argumentation.
cards.a: A claim is a debatable statement that the writer asks the audience to accept and then supports with evidence and reasoning. If no reasonable person could disagree with it, it is a fact, not a claim.
cards.n: The AP test for a claim is disagreement: if nobody could argue the other side, it cannot anchor an essay.

cards.q: Contrast a claim, a thesis, and an assertion.
cards.a: A claim is any debatable statement. A thesis is the single overarching claim that governs a whole text. An assertion is a statement offered without support - it becomes a claim only once evidence and reasoning back it.
cards.n: Readers penalize essays whose 'thesis' is really an unsupported assertion or a plain observation.

cards.q: Define a defensible thesis.
cards.a: A defensible thesis is a specific, arguable position that can be supported with available evidence. It takes a stance, previews a line of reasoning, and could be reasonably contested by an informed reader.
cards.n: Row A of every AP Lang rubric is won or lost here: defensible means arguable, not merely true.

cards.q: Identify what makes a thesis statement NOT defensible.
cards.a: It restates the prompt, states an obvious fact, merely announces a topic ('This essay will discuss...'), lists rhetorical devices with no message, or is so broad ('Since the dawn of time...') that no evidence could test it.
cards.n: Restating the prompt is the single most common Row A zero on the AP Lang exam.

cards.q: Define a claim of fact and give an example.
cards.a: A claim of fact argues that something is, was, or will be true, and is settled by evidence. Example: 'Standardized test scores have declined nationally since 2019.'
cards.n: A claim of fact still has to be arguable; if no reasonable reader could dispute it, it is a statement of fact and not a claim.

cards.q: Define a claim of value and give an example.
cards.a: A claim of value argues that something is good or bad, moral or immoral, better or worse, and depends on stated criteria. Example: 'Mandatory standardized testing is unfair to low-income students.'
cards.n: A value claim is only as strong as its criteria; strong writers name the standard they are judging by.

cards.q: Define a claim of policy and give an example.
cards.a: A claim of policy argues that a specific action should or should not be taken, and normally uses 'should' or 'must.' Example: 'States should stop requiring the SAT for public university admission.'
cards.n: Policy claims carry a hidden burden: you must show a problem exists AND that your solution is feasible.

cards.q: Decide the claim type: 'Social media harms adolescent mental health more than television ever did.'
cards.a: A claim of cause - the verb 'harms' asserts that social media directly produces (and produces more of) the mental-health damage than television did, which requires evidence ruling out other explanations, not just data confirming a plain fact.
cards.n: Comparative causal claims carry a double burden: show the harm exists and show it exceeds the harm from the thing compared.

cards.q: Explain the role of a subclaim in an essay.
cards.a: A subclaim is a smaller arguable statement that supports the thesis; each body paragraph usually advances one. Together the subclaims form the line of reasoning that makes the thesis persuasive.
cards.n: Subclaims have to be arguable too, so a paragraph that opens by announcing its topic rather than asserting a point has none.

cards.q: Define evidence and state what it must do in an argument.
cards.a: Evidence is the specific material - data, examples, testimony, texts, experience - offered to support a claim. It must be relevant to the claim, sufficient in amount, and accurate, and it must be interpreted, not just dropped in.
cards.n: Relevant, sufficient, accurate: use these three words when a prompt asks you to assess evidence.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of statistical evidence.
cards.a: Strength: statistics feel objective, scale up beyond one case, and persuade skeptical or data-minded audiences. Limits: they can be cherry-picked, decontextualized, or drawn from biased samples, and numbers alone do not establish causation.
cards.n: In MC questions, correlational data offered as proof of cause is a favorite wrong-reasoning trap.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of anecdotal evidence.
cards.a: Strength: an anecdote is concrete, memorable, and emotionally engaging, so it humanizes abstract claims. Limit: one story is a sample of one and cannot establish a trend, which makes it vulnerable to the charge of hasty generalization.
cards.n: Anecdote plus data is the strong combination: the story makes the number matter.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of expert testimony.
cards.a: Strength: borrowing a credentialed authority's ethos lends credibility on technical questions the audience cannot judge alone. Limit: it collapses if the expert is outside their field, biased, financially interested, or contradicted by other experts.
cards.n: Expert testimony is legitimate; appeal to authority is the fallacy version, where credentials replace reasons.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of analogy as evidence.
cards.a: Strength: an analogy makes an unfamiliar idea intelligible by mapping it onto something the audience already accepts. Limit: it proves nothing on its own, and it fails if the two cases differ in the respect that actually matters.
cards.n: Analogy is an illustrative move, not a probative one; treat it as clarification plus a hypothesis.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of historical example as evidence.
cards.a: Strength: a historical case shows that something has actually happened and supplies precedent and shared cultural weight. Limit: circumstances differ across eras, so the writer must argue that the past case is genuinely parallel.
cards.n: Strong AP argument essays use history but explicitly justify the comparison instead of assuming it.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of personal experience as evidence.
cards.a: Strength: it grants firsthand authority and immediacy, especially on questions of lived effect. Limit: it is unverifiable, unrepresentative, and easy for an audience to dismiss as atypical.
cards.n: AP allows personal evidence on Q3, but it must be specific and analyzed - not a vague 'I have seen this happen.'

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of textual evidence.
cards.a: Strength: quoted or paraphrased text lets readers verify the claim against the source itself, which is essential in rhetorical analysis. Limit: quotations can be pulled out of context, over-quoted, or left unexplained.
cards.n: On Q2, textual evidence without commentary earns at most 1 of 4 in Row B.

cards.q: Decide which evidence type best persuades a skeptical policy audience and explain why.
cards.a: Data and expert testimony, because a skeptical policy audience wants verifiable scale and credentialed backing; anecdote is then added to make the numbers vivid rather than to carry the proof.
cards.n: Evidence selection is a rhetorical choice: the right evidence is the evidence that audience will accept.

cards.q: Contrast commentary and summary.
cards.a: Summary restates what the evidence says. Commentary explains what the evidence means, how it supports the claim, and why it matters. Commentary answers 'so what?'; summary answers only 'what?'
cards.n: The most common Row B ceiling on AP Lang essays is evidence plus summary instead of evidence plus commentary.

cards.q: Explain what a sentence of strong commentary must do.
cards.a: It must connect the specific evidence to the specific claim by naming the reasoning link - why this detail makes that claim more believable - and then tie back to the thesis or the writer's purpose.
cards.n: A reliable frame: 'This suggests... which supports... because...' Avoid 'This shows how important X is.'

cards.q: Define a warrant.
cards.a: A warrant is the underlying assumption, usually unstated, that licenses the move from evidence to claim - the principle that explains why this evidence counts as support for this claim.
cards.n: Test a warrant by asking: what would someone have to already believe for this evidence to prove this claim?

cards.q: Identify the warrant: 'The bridge is 70 years old, so it should be replaced.'
cards.a: The warrant is the unstated assumption that bridges of about 70 years old are unsafe or beyond their design life and that unsafe infrastructure ought to be replaced.
cards.n: Warrants are where audiences actually disagree, so an argument that stalls is usually stuck on an assumption neither side has stated.

cards.q: Define backing in the Toulmin model.
cards.a: Backing is additional support offered for the warrant itself - evidence or reasoning that justifies the underlying assumption when the audience is unlikely to grant it automatically.
cards.n: Backing is only called for when the warrant is contested, so an argument heavy with backing signals the writer expects resistance.

cards.q: Define a qualifier and give three examples.
cards.a: A qualifier limits the strength or scope of a claim, signaling how confident the writer is. Examples: 'usually,' 'in most urban districts,' 'likely.'
cards.n: Qualifiers make claims more defensible, not weaker: an unqualified absolute is easy to refute with one counterexample.

cards.q: Define the rebuttal (reservation) element of the Toulmin model.
cards.a: The rebuttal names the conditions under which the claim would not hold, or anticipates and answers the strongest objection to it.
cards.n: Naming your own exception looks like weakness but reads as confidence, and it keeps the objection from arriving as a surprise.

cards.q: State the six elements of the Toulmin model.
cards.a: Claim, data (grounds/evidence), warrant, backing, qualifier, and rebuttal.
cards.n: Claim-data-warrant is the working core; backing, qualifier, and rebuttal are the refinements.
x: claim data warrant backing qualifier rebuttal

cards.q: Define Rogerian argument.
cards.a: Rogerian argument seeks common ground rather than victory: it states the opposing view fairly and sympathetically first, identifies shared values and the contexts where the opponent is right, then proposes a position that serves both sides' interests.
cards.n: Best for hostile audiences; its signature move is genuine concession before advocacy.

cards.q: Contrast Rogerian and classical (Aristotelian) argument.
cards.a: Classical argument is adversarial and linear - assert, prove, refute, and win over an undecided audience. Rogerian argument is conciliatory - understand, concede, and negotiate a shared position with a resistant audience.
cards.n: Choosing between them is itself a rhetorical decision driven by audience hostility.

cards.q: State the five parts of classical (Aristotelian) arrangement in order.
cards.a: Exordium (introduction), narratio (statement of facts/background), confirmatio (proof of your case), refutatio (refutation of opposing views), peroratio (conclusion).
cards.n: Notice that refutation comes before the conclusion: address the counterargument, then close.

cards.q: Define the exordium.
cards.a: The exordium is the opening that hooks the audience and establishes the speaker's credibility and goodwill, preparing listeners to be receptive before the case begins.
cards.n: Goodwill comes first for a reason: an audience that distrusts the speaker will not credit whatever evidence follows.

cards.q: Define the narratio.
cards.a: The narratio supplies the background: the facts, context, and history of the issue, told in a way that already frames the case favorably.
cards.n: Nothing in a narratio is neutral; which facts get selected and the order they arrive in already lean the case one way.

cards.q: Define the confirmatio.
cards.a: The confirmatio is the main body of proof, where the speaker develops the argument by presenting claims, evidence, and reasoning in support of the thesis.
cards.n: This is where a passage normally keeps its strongest evidence, and where a Q2 essay spends most of its own length.

cards.q: Define the refutatio.
cards.a: The refutatio anticipates and answers opposing arguments, conceding what is reasonable and rebutting what is not, so the audience's objections are removed before the close.
cards.n: Its placement before the close is deliberate, since objections answered too late still leave doubt at the moment of decision.

cards.q: Define the peroratio.
cards.a: The peroratio is the conclusion: it summarizes the case, amplifies its stakes, and makes the final emotional appeal or call to action.
cards.n: This is the classical home of pathos, so a passage's most quotable emotional language often sits in its final paragraph.

cards.q: Contrast inductive and deductive reasoning.
cards.a: Induction moves from specific observations to a general, probable conclusion. Deduction moves from a general premise to a specific conclusion that must follow if the premises are true.
cards.n: Induction yields probability, deduction yields necessity - a distinction MC questions test directly.

cards.q: Define a syllogism and give an example.
cards.a: A syllogism is a deductive form with a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion. Example: All published editorials are opinion pieces (major); this column is a published editorial (minor); therefore this column is an opinion piece.
cards.n: A syllogism can be valid but unsound: valid form plus a false premise guarantees nothing about whether the conclusion is true.

cards.q: Define an enthymeme.
cards.a: An enthymeme is a syllogism with a premise left unstated because the audience is assumed to share it. Example: 'She should be trusted with the budget - she has never missed a deadline,' assuming punctual people handle money responsibly.
cards.n: Enthymemes are where warrants hide; naming the missing premise is a classic AP analysis move.

cards.q: Explain why writers use enthymemes rather than full syllogisms.
cards.a: Leaving a premise unstated is efficient and flattering: it lets the audience supply the assumption themselves, which makes them feel they reasoned to the conclusion and makes the shared value seem obvious rather than debatable.
cards.n: On Q2 an enthymeme is a gift: naming the premise the writer left unstated exposes the values shared with that audience.

cards.q: Define concession and refutation as argumentative moves.
cards.a: Concession grants that part of the opposing view has merit; refutation then shows why that view is nonetheless inadequate or outweighed. Used together, they build ethos and defuse objections.
cards.n: 'While it is true that... , the more pressing consideration is...' is the standard concession-refutation frame.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of ad hominem and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Attacking the person making the argument instead of the argument itself. Example: 'You cannot take her climate proposal seriously - she flies private jets.'
cards.n: Not every personal remark is this fallacy; naming a real conflict of interest attacks credibility on grounds that are relevant.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of straw man and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Misrepresenting an opponent's position as a weaker or more extreme version, then refuting that version. Example: 'My opponent wants to cut the arts budget, so apparently she thinks music is worthless.'
cards.n: On an FRQ, quote the distortion and state what the opponent actually said, because the label by itself earns no credit.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of false dilemma (either/or) and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Presenting only two options when more exist. Example: 'Either we ban phones in school or we accept that students will never learn.'
cards.n: The tell is a forced either or or, and the refutation is simply naming the third option the writer left off the list.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of slippery slope and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Claiming one step will inevitably trigger a chain ending in disaster, without showing the links. Example: 'If we allow late homework, soon no one will turn in anything at all.'
cards.n: A slope argument is not automatically fallacious; it fails only when the writer never shows why each step has to lead to the next.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of hasty generalization and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Drawing a broad conclusion from a sample too small or unrepresentative to support it. Example: 'Two students cheated on the exam, so this generation has no integrity.'
cards.n: This fallacy is about sample size, while stereotyping is what happens when the overbroad conclusion gets applied back to an individual.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of post hoc ergo propter hoc and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Assuming that because B followed A, A caused B. Example: 'Test scores rose after we repainted the school, so the paint improved learning.'
cards.n: Sequence in time is not proof of production, which is why a claim of cause has to rule out the other explanations first.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of circular reasoning (begging the question) and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Assuming in the premises the very conclusion being argued for. Example: 'This novel is the greatest of the decade because no other book from the decade is as good.'
cards.n: The test is whether any independent support remains once the conclusion is removed; in circular reasoning nothing is left.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of appeal to authority (fallacious) and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Treating a person's status as proof, when they are outside their expertise or the claim needs evidence. Example: 'A famous actor endorses this supplement, so it must be effective.'
cards.n: Celebrity endorsement is the obvious version; the subtler one is a genuine expert speaking confidently outside their own field.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of appeal to popularity (bandwagon) and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Arguing something is true or right because many people believe or do it. Example: 'Millions of users can't be wrong - the app must be safe.'
cards.n: Popularity is relevant evidence for a claim about what people prefer, never for a claim about whether something is true.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of appeal to fear and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Substituting an alarming consequence for evidence in order to force agreement. Example: 'Vote against this measure or your family will not be safe in this town.'
cards.n: Fear is legitimate pathos when the danger is documented; the fallacy lies in substituting the alarm for proof that it is real.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of appeal to tradition and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Arguing that something is right or best because it has always been done that way. Example: 'We have opened with the same ceremony for ninety years, so it should not change.'
cards.n: Its mirror image is the appeal to novelty, which treats new as automatically better; both skip the question of what actually works.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of appeal to ignorance and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Claiming something is true because it has not been proven false, or false because unproven. Example: 'No study has proven the additive harmful, so it is perfectly safe.'
cards.n: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, and the burden of proof stays with whoever makes the positive claim.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of red herring and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Introducing an irrelevant issue to divert attention from the actual question. Example: 'You ask about the budget shortfall, but what about how well our team played this season?'
cards.n: A red herring changes the subject while a straw man distorts it, so the test is whether the reply addresses the original question at all.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of non sequitur and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Drawing a conclusion that does not follow logically from the premises given. Example: 'She reads a great deal, so she would make an excellent treasurer.'
cards.n: Non sequitur is the broad category, so name the narrower fallacy whenever one fits and save this label for gaps with no better name.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of equivocation and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Shifting the meaning of a key term partway through the argument. Example: 'Only man is rational; no woman is a man; therefore no woman is rational.'
cards.n: Equivocation hides inside valid-looking form, which is how a syllogism can be structurally perfect and still prove nothing.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of false analogy and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Comparing two things that differ in the respect essential to the argument. Example: 'Running a country is just like running a household budget, so the nation should never borrow.'
cards.n: Analogies are illustrations, not proofs; the counter is to name the one difference that matters to the conclusion being drawn.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of composition and division and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Composition assumes what is true of the parts is true of the whole; division assumes what is true of the whole is true of each part. Example: 'Every player is a star, so the team is unbeatable' (composition); 'It is a wealthy nation, so its citizens are wealthy' (division).
cards.n: A mnemonic: composition composes a whole out of parts, division divides a whole into parts, and both assume traits travel along.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of loaded question and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Asking a question that presupposes an unproven claim, so any direct answer concedes it. Example: 'Why does the administration keep wasting student fees?'
cards.n: The defense is to refuse the question and challenge its assumption, because answering either yes or no already grants the premise.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of tu quoque and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Deflecting criticism by charging the critic with the same fault, as if that answered the claim. Example: 'You say I should recycle, but you drive to work every day.'
cards.n: Tu quoque is a subtype of ad hominem, and hypocrisy in the critic leaves the truth of the criticism entirely untouched.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of no true Scotsman and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Rescuing a generalization from counterexamples by redefining the category to exclude them. Example: 'No serious scientist doubts this. - Dr. Vance does. - Then he is not a serious scientist.'
cards.n: The move makes the claim unfalsifiable: once any counterexample can be defined away, no evidence could ever count against it.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of cherry picking and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Citing only the data that supports the claim while suppressing contrary evidence. Example: 'Sales rose in March and June, proving the campaign worked' - omitting the four months sales fell.
cards.n: The damage here is to sufficiency rather than accuracy, since every fact cited can be true while the picture built from them is false.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of moving the goalposts and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Dismissing evidence that meets the agreed standard by demanding a new, higher one. Example: 'Fine, the trial worked, but I will not accept it until it is replicated in ten countries.'
cards.n: The tell is that the standard changes only once it has been met, so note what was originally demanded before the demand shifted.

cards.q: Explain how to write about a fallacy in an essay without simply naming it.
cards.a: Name the move, quote the specific words that make it, explain what the reasoning assumes or skips, and state the effect on the audience. Naming alone is labeling; the analysis is in the gap you expose.
cards.n: MC questions rarely ask for fallacy names; they ask what a passage's reasoning fails to establish.

cards.q: State the five classical canons of rhetoric.
cards.a: Invention, arrangement, style, memory, and delivery - the five arts ancient rhetoricians used to compose and deliver a speech, from finding arguments to the final performance.
cards.n: AP Lang draws heavily on arrangement and style; invention maps onto claims and evidence.

cards.q: Define invention as a canon of rhetoric.
cards.a: The process of discovering and developing the arguments, evidence, and lines of reasoning available for a given issue and audience - generating what to say before deciding how to say it.
cards.n: Invention is where a blank-page essay is won or lost; two minutes generating options beats writing down the first idea that arrives.

cards.q: Define delivery as a canon of rhetoric.
cards.a: The manner in which a speech is physically performed - voice, gesture, pacing, presence - as opposed to the words themselves; in written rhetoric it maps loosely onto formatting and tone of presentation.
cards.n: Delivery is the canon AP Lang tests least, since the exam hands you printed passages rather than performances to judge.

cards.q: Contrast a valid argument and a sound argument.
cards.a: An argument is valid if its conclusion follows logically from its premises, regardless of whether the premises are true. It is sound only if it is valid AND all its premises are actually true.
cards.n: A perfectly valid syllogism built on a false premise proves nothing about reality - a classic MC trap.

cards.q: Identify the type of reasoning: 'Every cygnet observed this spring on the lake was white, so the town's swans are a white species.'
cards.a: Inductive reasoning. It moves from a set of specific observed instances to a general, merely probable conclusion about the whole category.
cards.n: The classic rebuttal to this pattern is the black swan, one case that overturns a generalization built from many observations.

cards.q: Identify the type of reasoning: 'All municipal bonds are tax-exempt. This is a municipal bond. Therefore this bond is tax-exempt.'
cards.a: Deductive reasoning. It moves from a general premise through a specific case to a conclusion that must be true if the premises are true.
cards.n: Validity and truth are separate: this form stays valid even if the first premise is false, but the argument is then unsound.

cards.q: Contrast a primary and a secondary source.
cards.a: A primary source is firsthand: original data, a speech transcript, an eyewitness account, a raw document. A secondary source analyzes or reports on primary material, such as a journalist's summary of a study.
cards.n: On the synthesis essay, naming a source as primary or secondary can support a claim about its reliability.

cards.q: Define a spurious (false) correlation and give an example.
cards.a: A statistical association between two variables with no real causal connection, often produced by coincidence or a hidden third factor. e.g. ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer because of heat, not each other.
cards.n: This is the statistical version of post hoc reasoning - correlation mistaken for causation.

cards.q: Decide the claim type: 'Requiring a civics course should not be optional for graduation.'
cards.a: A claim of policy. It uses should and urges a specific action, rather than asserting a fact or judging worth in the abstract.
cards.n: Policy claims carry the heaviest burden of the five, needing both a demonstrated problem and a remedy that would actually address it.

cards.q: Decide the claim type: 'A four-day school week is worse for working families than a traditional schedule.'
cards.a: A claim of value. It judges the schedule as worse against an implied standard (impact on working families) rather than asserting a checkable fact or urging an action.
cards.n: Value claims stand or fall on the standard behind them, so naming that standard explicitly is what makes one defensible.

cards.q: Define burden of proof in argumentation.
cards.a: The obligation to provide sufficient evidence and reasoning for a claim before an audience is required to accept it. The burden rests on whoever makes the claim, especially one that departs from the status quo.
cards.n: A policy claim proposing change carries a heavier burden of proof than one defending current practice.

cards.q: Define data (grounds) in the Toulmin model.
cards.a: Data, or grounds, is the specific evidence or facts offered as the foundation for a claim - the concrete support the warrant then links to that claim.
cards.n: Grounds is the Toulmin term for what the rest of the deck calls evidence.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Senator Cole wants stricter emissions limits, but why listen to someone who just bought a second house?'
cards.a: Ad hominem. It attacks Senator Cole's personal choices instead of addressing the merits of the emissions proposal.
cards.n: A relevance test settles it quickly: does owning a second house change what the emissions data show? If not, the attack is beside the point.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'She wants schools to teach media literacy, which just means she thinks students are too dumb to think for themselves.'
cards.a: Straw man. It replaces the actual proposal with an exaggerated, easier-to-attack version and refutes that instead.
cards.n: The word just often flags the distortion, compressing a proposal down into a motive the proposer never actually claimed.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Either we privatize the water utility, or the whole system collapses within a year.'
cards.a: False dilemma. It presents only two extreme outcomes when other options, such as partial reform or new funding, are available.
cards.n: Refute one by naming a specific third path rather than by saying more options exist; the named alternative is what does the work.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'If we let students redo one quiz, soon every assignment will be optional and no one will learn anything.'
cards.a: Slippery slope. It claims one small allowance will inevitably cascade into total collapse without showing why each step must follow.
cards.n: Ask which link is weakest: the jump from one retaken quiz to every assignment is where this chain actually breaks.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'I met two rude tourists from that city, so people from there must all be unfriendly.'
cards.a: Hasty generalization. It draws a sweeping conclusion about an entire population from a sample of two encounters.
cards.n: Sample size is one problem, but the leap from tourists to residents adds an unrepresentative-sample problem on top of it.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'The team started winning right after they changed the mascot, so the new mascot must be the reason.'
cards.a: Post hoc ergo propter hoc. It assumes the earlier event caused the later one merely because it came first.
cards.n: Roster changes, an easier schedule or ordinary luck could all explain the wins, and the mascot claim never rules any of them out.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'This painting is a masterpiece because a true genius made it, and we know she's a genius because look at this masterpiece.'
cards.a: Circular reasoning (begging the question). The conclusion is used to prove the premise, which is then used to prove the conclusion again.
cards.n: Compressed into one sentence the circle is easy to see; in real arguments it usually spans several paragraphs and hides.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'This diet must work - a famous actor swears by it in every interview.'
cards.a: Appeal to authority (fallacious). The actor's fame, not any relevant nutritional expertise, is offered as proof the diet works.
cards.n: The fix is not to distrust all testimony but to ask whether the source's expertise actually matches the claim being made.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Everyone at school already has the new phone, so obviously you need one too.'
cards.a: Bandwagon (appeal to popularity). It treats widespread adoption as proof that owning the phone is necessary or correct.
cards.n: Bandwagon often hides inside the word obviously, which asserts that everyone agrees instead of giving a reason to agree.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Why worry about the factory's emissions when there's so much litter downtown nobody cleans up?'
cards.a: Red herring. It diverts attention from the emissions question to an unrelated issue instead of addressing the original point.
cards.n: The rhetorical question form does the diverting work here, making a change of subject feel like a fair counterpoint.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'You say I text too much at dinner, but you're always checking email at the table too.'
cards.a: Tu quoque. It deflects the criticism by accusing the critic of the same behavior instead of answering whether it is valid.
cards.n: Both people can be wrong at the same time, which is why a charge of hypocrisy never settles whether the original complaint was right.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'A light diet is better for you, and light things are easier to lift, so a light diet makes you stronger.'
cards.a: Equivocation. The word light shifts meaning midargument from low in calories to low in weight, so the reasoning only appears to connect.
cards.n: Underline the repeated term and write its meaning at each appearance; if the two meanings differ, the argument is equivocating.

cards.q: Contrast what the Toulmin model and classical arrangement are each used for.
cards.a: Classical arrangement structures an entire speech or essay into ordered parts, while the Toulmin model breaks down the logical structure of a single claim wherever it appears.
cards.n: Students sometimes treat Toulmin as a rival organizational scheme for an essay, but it was designed to test logic, not replace an outline.
x: structuring a speech vs. testing one claim's logic

cards.q: Explain when a writer would use Toulmin analysis rather than classical arrangement while planning an argument essay.
cards.a: Toulmin analysis helps a writer test whether one claim's reasoning actually holds up before writing, while classical arrangement helps organize the finished sequence of the whole essay.
cards.n: A warrant your audience turns out to reject is a reason to change the claim, not just to move it later in the essay.

cards.q: Decide which argument structure fits: a writer wants to find common ground with a skeptical audience before proposing any solution.
cards.a: Rogerian argument; it opens by acknowledging the opposing view's validity, which classical arrangement's confrontational structure is not built to do first.
cards.n: Rogerian argument is named for psychologist Carl Rogers, whose model of listening before replying the structure borrows.

cards.q: Define hedging language and give an example.
cards.a: Wording that softens a claim to avoid full commitment, such as 'it could be argued' or 'some might say,' often used to dodge rather than sharpen a position.
cards.n: Hedging is not the same as being appropriately cautious; the problem is vagueness, not caution itself.

cards.q: Contrast a qualifier that strengthens an argument and hedging language that weakens one.
cards.a: A precise qualifier narrows exactly when and where a claim holds, showing control, while hedging language avoids commitment altogether, leaving the reader unsure what the writer believes.
cards.n: 'Under most circumstances' qualifies; 'it could maybe be said' hedges - the difference is whether the limit is specific.

cards.q: Identify the problem: 'Some people might think that social media could possibly be somewhat harmful in certain cases.'
cards.a: Excessive hedging; stacking 'might,' 'could possibly,' and 'somewhat' buries any actual claim under vague qualification.
cards.n: Hedging and qualifying look alike but do opposite work: a qualifier names the conditions under which a claim holds, a hedge names none.

cards.q: Explain where a concession is most effective when placed within a body paragraph.
cards.a: Early in the paragraph, before the writer's own point, so the refutation that follows gets the final, more memorable word.
cards.n: Placing the concession first also signals fairness to the reader before the writer starts pushing back.

cards.q: Explain the risk of placing a concession at the very end of an argument essay.
cards.a: Ending on the opposing view without refuting it can leave the reader's last impression favoring the counterargument instead of the writer's own thesis.
cards.n: Final sentences carry disproportionate weight, which is exactly why classical arrangement puts the refutatio before the peroratio.

cards.q: Apply a qualifier to strengthen this claim: 'Standardized tests are unfair to low-income students.'
cards.a: Add a scope qualifier: 'Standardized tests are unfair to low-income students when access to test preparation is unequal,' narrowing the claim to what evidence can support.
cards.n: A vague qualifier like 'sometimes' would do less work than naming the actual condition, unequal access to test prep.

cards.q: Decide the type of reasoning: 'Every bridge inspected this year showed rust damage, so the county's bridges are likely deteriorating faster than reports admit.'
cards.a: Inductive reasoning; a general conclusion is drawn from a pattern in specific observed cases, so it is probable rather than certain.
cards.n: The word 'likely' in the conclusion is itself a clue that the reasoning is inductive rather than certain.

cards.q: Decide the type of reasoning: 'All published city audits must be reviewed by the comptroller. This audit was published. Therefore this audit must be reviewed by the comptroller.'
cards.a: Deductive reasoning; the conclusion follows necessarily from the two premises, in the form of a syllogism.
cards.n: The modal has to carry through. Concluding 'therefore the comptroller reviewed it' would not follow - a rule that something must happen is not evidence that it did.

cards.q: Decide the type of reasoning: 'Three of the last four mayors raised taxes in their first year, so the new mayor probably will too.'
cards.a: Inductive reasoning; the prediction is drawn from a pattern of past cases, so it is likely but not guaranteed.
cards.n: The word probably is doing honest work here; rewritten as certainly, the same sentence would overstate what a pattern of cases shows.

cards.q: Explain why an inductive argument can be strong even though its conclusion is never certain.
cards.a: Strength in inductive reasoning comes from the size and representativeness of the sample, not from logical necessity; better evidence makes the conclusion more probable, not proven.
cards.n: A single well-chosen counterexample can still weaken even a large inductive sample, which is why induction stays probabilistic.

cards.q: Apply deductive reasoning to reach a conclusion: 'All municipal water systems must test for lead annually. Elm Creek runs a municipal water system.'
cards.a: Therefore Elm Creek must test its water for lead annually - the conclusion follows necessarily once both premises are accepted.
cards.n: Watch the scope of the first premise: if it read most systems rather than all, the conclusion would drop back to merely probable.

cards.q: Identify the classical canon most at work when a writer chooses which of five strong points to actually include in a tight time limit.
cards.a: Invention; deciding what material belongs in the argument at all happens in invention, before arrangement or style come into play.
cards.n: Invention happens before a word of the essay is drafted, which is why timed planning belongs to this canon.

cards.q: Explain why pairing a statistic with a brief anecdote often persuades better than either alone.
cards.a: The statistic supplies scope and credibility while the anecdote supplies a human stake, so the pairing satisfies both a skeptical reader's logos and an engaged reader's pathos.
cards.n: The same pairing is a reliable Q3 move, where one named example developed with commentary outperforms a list of general assertions.

cards.q: Decide whether this is a defensible claim or an unqualified overclaim: 'Homework should never be assigned on weekends.'
cards.a: An unqualified overclaim; 'never' forecloses any exception a reasonable opponent could raise, making the claim easy to defeat with a single counterexample.
cards.n: Swapping 'never' for 'rarely,' or naming a specific condition, would make the same claim far harder to attack.

cards.q: Contrast how concession is used in Rogerian argument versus in classical refutation.
cards.a: Rogerian argument opens with a genuine concession to build trust before any claim is made, while classical refutation raises the opposing view only after the writer's own case, mainly to dismantle it.
cards.n: The order matters more than the content: the same concession lands very differently depending on where it sits.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'This new bridge inspection policy must be flawed, since it was proposed by a councilman who once missed a budget deadline.'
cards.a: Ad hominem; the policy is dismissed by attacking the proposer's past record instead of addressing the policy's actual merits.
cards.h: → attacks the proposer, not the policy
cards.n: Notice the policy itself never gets addressed at all; that total silence on the merits is the fallacy's signature.

cards.q: Decide which evidence type best supports a claim about a long-term historical trend, and explain why.
cards.a: Historical example; a documented pattern across past cases shows the trend is not a one-time coincidence, which a single statistic or anecdote cannot demonstrate alone.
cards.n: Match evidence to the shape of the claim: claims about patterns over time need several cases, claims about scale need numbers.

cards.q: Explain why a writer might choose Rogerian argument over classical arrangement when addressing a hostile audience.
cards.a: Rogerian argument's opening concession lowers a hostile audience's defenses before any claim is made, while classical arrangement's direct confirmatio can read as combative and shut the audience down early.
cards.n: A hostile audience that feels attacked from the first sentence rarely reads far enough to hear the strongest evidence.

cards.q: Define arrangement as a canon of rhetoric.
cards.a: The canon governing how a speaker organizes ideas into an effective structure, deciding the order in which claims, evidence, and appeals appear for maximum impact.
cards.n: This is the same organizational thinking behind classical arrangement, just named as one of the five canons.

cards.q: Define style as a canon of rhetoric.
cards.a: The canon governing word choice, sentence structure, and figurative language, and how a speaker adapts these to purpose, audience, and occasion.
cards.n: This canon-level 'style' is the same concept the Style unit expands into devices, syntax, and tone.

cards.q: Define memory as a canon of rhetoric.
cards.a: The canon governing a speaker's preparation to deliver a speech without total reliance on a written text, historically through memorization techniques, and now also internalizing an argument well enough to adapt it live.
cards.n: Memory is the canon AP Lang tests least directly, since the exam is written, not delivered aloud.

cards.q: Contrast the canon of invention and the canon of arrangement.
cards.a: Invention is the process of discovering what to say - generating arguments, evidence, and appeals. Arrangement is the separate process of deciding the order in which that already-discovered material should appear.
cards.n: A timed essay collapses the two, but the split still helps: running out of ideas is an invention problem, not an outline problem.

cards.q: State which classical canon governs a writer's decision to open with an emotional story rather than a statistic.
cards.a: Arrangement - the canon that governs the order and placement of material, including which piece of evidence leads.
cards.n: Invention would cover choosing the story and statistic in the first place; arrangement covers which comes first.

cards.q: Contrast a warrant and its backing in the Toulmin model.
cards.a: The warrant is the usually unstated assumption that connects the data to the claim. The backing is the further support offered if that warrant itself is challenged.
cards.h: → the assumption vs support for the assumption
cards.n: A warrant can be left implicit; backing is what you supply once someone asks why they should accept it.

cards.q: Identify the warrant: 'She graduated from a top engineering program, so she is qualified for the job.'
cards.a: The unstated assumption that graduating from a top engineering program indicates job qualification - that program prestige reliably predicts competence.
cards.n: Warrants are usually left unstated on purpose - saying one aloud that the audience does not share can backfire.

cards.q: Apply the Toulmin model: identify the data and claim in 'The reservoir dropped four feet, so the city should introduce watering restrictions.'
cards.a: Data (grounds): the reservoir dropped four feet this summer. Claim: the city should introduce watering restrictions.
cards.n: The warrant is the missing third piece: that a four-foot drop signals a shortage serious enough to justify restricting use.

cards.q: Explain why a rebuttal (reservation) makes a Toulmin argument stronger rather than weaker.
cards.a: Naming the specific conditions under which the claim would not hold shows the writer has tested the argument's limits, which makes the parts that do hold more credible, not less.
cards.n: This is the Toulmin-model version of a qualifier or concession elsewhere in argumentation.

cards.q: Define circumstantial evidence and give an example.
cards.a: Evidence that suggests a conclusion indirectly through surrounding facts rather than proving it directly, such as inferring a store was closed from its dark windows and empty parking lot rather than a posted sign.
cards.n: Circumstantial evidence can be persuasive in volume but is weaker than direct evidence alone.

cards.q: Define precedent as a form of evidence.
cards.a: A prior decision, event, or established practice cited to support how a current or future case should be treated, on the logic that like cases deserve like treatment.
cards.h: → prior case used to justify a new one
cards.n: Precedent is common in legal and policy arguments but weaker when the two cases differ in a way that matters.
x: a prior case used to justify a new one

cards.q: Contrast quantitative and qualitative evidence.
cards.a: Quantitative evidence is numerical - statistics, measurements, survey percentages. Qualitative evidence is descriptive - interviews, observations, case studies - capturing nuance numbers alone can miss.
cards.n: A strong Q1 synthesis essay often pairs one quantitative source with one qualitative source rather than relying on only one kind.

cards.q: Define a case study as a form of evidence and note its main limitation.
cards.a: An in-depth examination of one instance, person, or event used to illustrate a broader claim. Its limitation is that a single case may not generalize to the wider population.
cards.n: That limitation is an opening for the other side, so a writer leaning on one case usually pairs it with broader data.

cards.q: Decide the stronger evidence for a claim that a new policy is effective nationwide: one detailed case study, or a smaller statistic drawn from many locations.
cards.a: The multi-location statistic, because it demonstrates the effect holds across contexts. A single case study is vivid but cannot show the pattern generalizes.
cards.n: Vividness and representativeness are different strengths - a case study wins the first, a broad statistic wins the second.

cards.q: Define a claim of cause and give an example.
cards.a: A claim asserting that one thing brings about another, such as 'Reduced recess time has caused a rise in childhood anxiety.' It requires evidence of a causal link, not just a correlation.
cards.n: Claims of cause are the easiest claim type to overreach on - correlation is not causation.

cards.q: Define a claim of definition and give an example.
cards.a: A claim asserting how a term or category should be understood, such as 'Vaping counts as tobacco use under the school's policy.' The argument turns on establishing criteria for the category.
cards.n: Definition claims decide which rules apply, so they are often the hidden first move inside a policy or legal argument.

cards.q: Decide the claim type: 'The plant closure caused unemployment to double in the county within a year.'
cards.a: A claim of cause - it asserts that one event directly produced another, which requires evidence ruling out other explanations.
cards.n: Watch for claims of cause disguised as claims of fact - a causal verb like 'caused' is the giveaway.

cards.q: Explain why a claim of cause needs stronger evidence than a claim of value to be defensible.
cards.a: A claim of cause must rule out coincidence and other explanations to show one thing actually produced another, while a claim of value only needs to justify a judgment against stated criteria, a lower evidentiary bar.
cards.h: → ruling out alternatives vs justifying a judgment
cards.n: Correlation is the shortcut usually taken here: two things moving together is evidence that a cause may exist, not that it does.

cards.q: Define a necessary condition and a sufficient condition, and give an example distinguishing them.
cards.a: A necessary condition must be true for an outcome to occur, though it may not guarantee it; a sufficient condition guarantees the outcome on its own. Being 16 is necessary for a driver's license in most states but not sufficient, since passing the test is also required.
cards.h: → must happen vs guarantees it happens
cards.n: Confusing the two is a common source of invalid syllogisms on the exam.

cards.q: Explain the logical error of affirming the consequent in a conditional argument.
cards.a: Given 'if A then B,' affirming the consequent wrongly concludes A from the mere fact that B is true, ignoring that B could have other causes. Wet grass does not prove it rained, since a sprinkler could explain it too.
cards.h: → B being true doesn't prove A
cards.n: Its valid twin is modus tollens, where B being false does prove A is false; only the affirming direction of the move fails.

cards.q: Identify the classical arrangement part: an essay's final paragraph issues a call to action and leaves a resonant final image.
cards.a: The peroratio - the concluding part of classical arrangement that sums up the argument and makes a final emotional appeal to move the audience to action.
cards.n: The peroratio is often where a writer risks overreaching with pathos after a carefully reasoned confirmatio.

cards.q: Contrast the narratio and the confirmatio in classical arrangement.
cards.a: The narratio lays out the background facts a reader needs to understand the dispute; the confirmatio presents the actual arguments and evidence supporting the writer's claim.
cards.h: → background facts vs the actual case
cards.n: Students often skip a narratio, but a reader who lacks context cannot fairly judge the confirmatio that follows.

cards.q: Define a line of reasoning.
cards.a: A line of reasoning is the logical sequence of claims and supporting evidence that connects the thesis to the conclusion - the order in which ideas build so that each paragraph makes the next one possible.
cards.n: Row B rewards a line of reasoning: paragraphs in an arbitrary order cost points even when each is well written.

cards.q: Explain how to test whether an essay has a line of reasoning.
cards.a: Read only the topic sentences in order. If they form a coherent argument that arrives at the thesis, the line of reasoning holds; if they read as an unordered list of observations, it does not.
cards.n: This topic-sentence test is the fastest self-check in the final minutes of an FRQ.

cards.q: Explain the function of a topic sentence.
cards.a: A topic sentence states the paragraph's subclaim and links it to the thesis, telling the reader what this paragraph will prove and why it comes here. It should assert, not announce or summarize the source.
cards.n: 'In source B, the author discusses cost' is an announcement; a topic sentence must make an arguable point.

cards.q: Define unity in a paragraph.
cards.a: Unity means every sentence in the paragraph supports the single idea named in the topic sentence; nothing wanders into a different claim.
cards.n: The usual cause of lost unity is a good sentence the writer did not want to cut; if it proves a different point, it belongs elsewhere.

cards.q: Define coherence in writing.
cards.a: Coherence means the sentences and paragraphs connect so the reader can follow the movement of thought, achieved through transitions, repeated key terms, pronoun reference, and consistent order.
cards.n: Unity is about what belongs in a paragraph and coherence about whether the order can be followed, so an essay can have one without the other.

cards.q: Explain the standard structure of an argumentative body paragraph.
cards.a: Topic sentence stating the subclaim; specific evidence introduced with context; commentary explaining how the evidence proves the subclaim; and a link sentence tying the subclaim back to the thesis or forward to the next.
cards.n: Aim for at least two sentences of commentary for every one sentence of evidence.

cards.q: Decide when to start a new paragraph.
cards.a: Start a new paragraph when the subclaim changes, when a new source or piece of evidence requires its own analysis, when shifting from your case to the counterargument, or when a paragraph has grown so long the reader loses the claim.
cards.n: On a timed essay, breaks also buy readability: a reader working through hundreds of booklets finds a claim fastest at the top of one.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal addition and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Addition: furthermore, moreover, in addition, also, likewise. They signal to the reader that what follows adds another item of the same kind.
cards.n: These are the easiest transitions to overuse, since stacking furthermore and moreover makes a list look like reasoning without advancing it.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal contrast and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Contrast: however, yet, nevertheless, on the other hand, conversely. They signal to the reader that what follows opposes or turns against what came before.
cards.n: However needs a semicolon before it when it joins two independent clauses, and a comma alone in that spot creates a comma splice.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal causation and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Causation: therefore, consequently, thus, as a result, because. They signal to the reader that what follows is the cause or the effect of what came before.
cards.n: Because subordinates while therefore does not, so the punctuation differs: one joins clauses directly, the other needs a semicolon or period.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal concession and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Concession: admittedly, granted, of course, to be sure, while it is true that. They signal to the reader that what follows grants a point to the other side before it is answered.
cards.n: These words promise a turn, so a reader waits for the but or yet that follows; a concession left without one reads as surrender.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal exemplification and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Exemplification: for example, for instance, specifically, to illustrate, namely. They signal to the reader that what follows is a specific instance of the general claim.
cards.n: For example promises a case that fits the claim just made, which makes a mismatched example more damaging than no example at all.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal sequence and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Sequence: first, next, subsequently, meanwhile, finally. They signal to the reader that what follows comes next in an order of steps, stages, or priority.
cards.n: Sequence words describe order without proving connection, so first, second and third can hide the absence of a line of reasoning.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal emphasis and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Emphasis: indeed, above all, in fact, most significantly, especially. They signal to the reader that what follows is the most important point so far.
cards.n: These transitions make a claim about rank, so using one on every point flattens the very hierarchy they exist to create.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal conclusion and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Conclusion: in short, ultimately, on the whole, in conclusion, therefore. They signal to the reader that what follows closes the argument or sums it up.
cards.n: In conclusion is the weakest of these on a timed essay, because it announces the ending instead of doing anything with it.

cards.q: Explain the most common misuse of transitions.
cards.a: Using a transition whose relationship the sentences do not actually have - most often 'however' between two agreeing sentences or 'therefore' where no cause was established. The word then signals a logic the paragraph never performs.
cards.n: MC revision questions frequently test exactly this: the right answer replaces a mismatched connective.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called narration and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Narration: Tells a sequence of events as a story. It is best for making an abstract problem concrete and building emotional engagement.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: A narrative works as evidence only when the writer ties it back to the claim; left to stand alone it reads as a digression.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called description and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Description: Renders sensory and concrete detail about a subject. It is best for making a scene or condition vivid so the audience can judge it firsthand.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Description argues through what it selects: a scene rendered in sensory detail invites the verdict without ever stating it.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called definition and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Definition: Establishes what a key term means and does not mean. It is best when the argument turns on a contested term such as 'freedom' or 'fairness'.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Whoever wins the definition often wins the argument, which is why contested policy debates so often open by fighting over one word.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called exemplification and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Exemplification: Supports a generalization with a series of specific instances. It is best for showing that a pattern is real and widespread rather than isolated.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Three well-chosen instances can persuade more than one developed one here, since the point being proved is that the pattern is not isolated.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called comparison-contrast and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Comparison-contrast: Sets two subjects side by side to reveal similarity or difference. It is best for evaluating alternatives; organized point-by-point or subject-by-subject.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Point-by-point keeps the comparison visible but fragments each subject, while subject-by-subject flows better and risks two loose summaries.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called cause-effect and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Cause-effect: Traces why something happened or what it produced. It is best for arguments about responsibility or consequence; must guard against post hoc reasoning.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Strong cause-effect writing names the mechanism joining the two, because a sequence with no mechanism is correlation in disguise.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called process analysis and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Process analysis: Explains the steps by which something happens or is done. It is best for showing feasibility or exposing where a system breaks down.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Explaining how something works is itself a way to argue, since laying out each step makes a system's failure point hard to deny.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called classification and division and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Classification and division: Sorts items into categories, or breaks one subject into parts. It is best for imposing order on a sprawling issue so each part can be judged separately.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: The categories have to be mutually exclusive and cover the ground, or the argument built on them will leak at the overlaps.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called problem-solution and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Problem-solution: Establishes a problem, then proposes and defends a remedy. It is best for policy arguments; the solution must be shown to be both effective and feasible.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Weak versions skip feasibility and propose a remedy no one could fund or enforce, which is the first thing the opposition names.

cards.q: Explain why identifying a passage's method of development matters in rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: The method is itself a rhetorical choice: choosing to define a term, narrate a case, or classify a field shapes what the audience sees as the issue. Naming the method lets you analyze the structure rather than only the sentence-level devices.
cards.n: Analyzing organization is a higher-level move than device-spotting and often supports the sophistication point.

cards.q: Explain what an effective introduction does on an AP Lang essay.
cards.a: It orients the reader to the issue in one or two sentences, narrows to the specific question at stake, and ends with a defensible thesis that previews the line of reasoning. Three to four sentences is plenty.
