cards.n: Read the line aloud to test it, and remember the effect only counts as analysis once it is tied to what the passage argues.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'The senator, a decorated veteran, refused to discuss the vote.'
cards.a: An appositive: 'a decorated veteran' renames senator, adding a credential in a compact aside rather than a full clause.
cards.n: Appositives let a writer smuggle in characterization or credibility without slowing the sentence with a new clause.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'The crowd fell silent, its collective breath held, as the verdict was read.'
cards.a: An absolute phrase: 'its collective breath held' modifies the whole main clause rather than a single noun, adding a vivid simultaneous detail.
cards.h: → noun + participle modifying the whole clause
cards.n: Absolute phrases modify the whole clause, not a single word, which is why they resist being folded into a simple adjective.

cards.q: Explain why a writer would set an appositive off with dashes instead of commas.
cards.a: Dashes make the appositive feel like an interruption or emphasis, drawing the reader's eye, while commas fold it in more quietly as background information.
cards.n: The grammar is identical either way; the punctuation choice is entirely about how much attention the aside should get.

cards.q: Explain the rhetorical effect of stacking two absolute phrases in one sentence.
cards.a: Stacked absolute phrases let a writer layer several simultaneous images or conditions onto one main action, creating a cinematic, slow-motion effect.
cards.n: Overusing this move across many sentences can feel overwritten, so save it for a single high-impact moment.

cards.q: Apply subordination to this pair to emphasize the job loss: 'The town lost its factory. Three hundred jobs disappeared overnight.'
cards.a: Subordinate the first idea: 'When the town lost its factory, three hundred jobs disappeared overnight,' putting the emphasis in the independent clause on the jobs.
cards.n: Whatever sits in the independent clause reads as the sentence's main point; the subordinate clause supplies background.

cards.q: Apply coordination to this pair to give both ideas equal weight: 'The mayor cut the ribbon. Protesters lined the sidewalk.'
cards.a: Coordinate them with a conjunction: 'The mayor cut the ribbon, and protesters lined the sidewalk,' which keeps both images equally prominent instead of subordinating either.
cards.n: Coordination claims the two events belong together, so the conjunction does argumentative work: and joins them, but sets them against each other.

cards.q: Contrast the rhetorical effect of a semicolon, a colon, and a dash used at the same junction in a sentence.
cards.a: A semicolon balances two equal, related ideas; a colon announces that an explanation or list is about to deliver on a promise; a dash breaks in for emphasis or an abrupt aside.
cards.n: Three punctuation marks can often connect the same two ideas, but each frames the reader's expectation differently.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The board had one option left: resign.'
cards.a: The colon sets up the single word 'resign' as a blunt, delayed payoff, giving it more weight than a comma would.
cards.n: A colon promises that what follows will deliver on what came before; here the promise is a one-word gut punch.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The vote was close; the consequences were not.'
cards.a: The semicolon signals that the two clauses are tightly related and worth weighing against each other, without subordinating either one.
cards.n: The compression is the point: a period would let the reader lose hold of the first clause before the second lands on it.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The plan was approved - barely - after three hours of debate.'
cards.a: The dashes interrupt the sentence to insert 'barely' as a pointed aside, forcing the reader to notice how narrow the approval was.
cards.n: Dashes read as more informal and abrupt than parentheses, which cushion an aside more gently.

cards.q: Contrast anaphora and epistrophe by where the repeated words fall.
cards.a: Anaphora repeats words at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences, while epistrophe repeats them at the end; anaphora drives forward and epistrophe hammers a close.
cards.n: Some passages use both at once, repeating a word at a clause's start and again at its end, so trace the repetition physically through the sentence.
x: repetition at the start vs. the end

cards.q: Identify the scheme in Lincoln's Gettysburg Address: 'we can not dedicate, we can not consecrate, we can not hallow this ground.'
cards.a: Anaphora; repeating 'we can not' at the start of each clause builds toward the admission that words cannot match the soldiers' sacrifice.
cards.n: Lincoln uses the anaphora to deflate the ceremony itself before redirecting attention to the unfinished work of the living.

cards.q: Identify the scheme in Kennedy's inaugural: 'we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship.'
cards.a: Parallelism — a tricolon of three matched verb-plus-object phrases with 'any' in the same slot each time. It is NOT anaphora: the clauses begin with pay, bear and meet, and anaphora needs the repeated word at the start of each clause.
cards.h: → name the scheme, and say why it is not anaphora
cards.n: A standing trap: repetition in the same position inside each clause is still not anaphora unless that position is the beginning.

cards.q: Identify the scheme in Lincoln's Gettysburg Address: 'government of the people, by the people, for the people.'
cards.a: A tricolon on parallel prepositional phrases, with 'the people' repeated at the end of each - closer to epistrophe than anaphora since the repetition lands at the close.
cards.n: This line is often mislabeled as anaphora; the repeated words fall at the end of each phrase, not the start.

cards.q: Identify the device in Kennedy's inaugural: 'Ask not what your country can do for you - ask what you can do for your country.'
cards.a: Antithesis and antimetabole - antimetabole being the chiasmus in which the identical words come back reversed: country/you, then you/country, sharpening the contrast between receiving and giving.
cards.n: Naming antimetabole rather than the broader chiasmus shows a reader you can see the exact structure, not just the contrast.

cards.q: Contrast the two devices at work in Kennedy's line 'ask not what your country can do for you - ask what you can do for your country.'
cards.a: It is antithesis because it opposes two contrasting ideas, and chiasmus because the second clause reverses the grammatical order of the first.
cards.n: A single line can carry more than one device at once; identify both the contrast and the mirrored structure.

cards.q: Identify the technique Swift leans on in A Modest Proposal by having an economist calmly recommend eating Irish infants.
cards.a: A sustained ironic persona whose deadpan logic exposes the real cruelty of English policy toward the Irish poor, rather than stating the criticism directly.
cards.n: The persona is the whole device, so quoting the narrator's cold arithmetic proves the irony better than quoting the shocking proposal.

cards.q: Identify the satire type in A Modest Proposal.
cards.a: Juvenalian satire; Swift's proposal is bitter and biting, using shocking irony to condemn real suffering rather than to gently amuse.
cards.n: Because the target is real, ongoing suffering rather than a mild social habit, calling this Horatian would badly undersell the essay's anger.

cards.q: Explain why A Modest Proposal's title is itself ironic.
cards.a: Calling a proposal to eat infants 'modest' signals from the first word that the speaker's calm reasonableness cannot be trusted, priming readers to look past the surface argument.
cards.n: Verbal irony operates here at the level of one adjective, which makes the title the cheapest quotable evidence in the whole essay.

cards.q: Define parody and give an example.
cards.a: A work that imitates another text's style or conventions closely enough to be recognized, exaggerating it for comic or critical effect.
cards.n: Parody depends on the audience recognizing the original; without that recognition the joke does not land.

cards.q: Define lampoon and give an example.
cards.a: A short, sharply mocking piece aimed at a specific person or institution, using ridicule rather than balanced argument to attack its target.
cards.n: Lampoon names the attack while satire names the mode, so a lampoon is satire aimed at one target with the gloves off.
x: a piece that ridicules a specific target

cards.q: Define caricature and give an example.
cards.a: A description or portrayal that exaggerates a subject's distinctive features or traits to make them ridiculous, often reducing a person to one exaggerated trait.
cards.n: Caricature works because the exaggerated trait is still recognizably drawn from something real about the subject.
x: exaggerated portrayal of a real subject

cards.q: Contrast parody and lampoon by what each one imitates.
cards.a: Parody imitates a text's style or form to mock it, while lampoon attacks a specific person or institution directly without needing to imitate anything.
cards.h: → imitates a form vs. attacks a target
cards.n: A single piece can do both at once: parody a genre while also lampooning a specific person writing within it.

cards.q: Contrast caricature and stereotype as satirical tools.
cards.a: Caricature exaggerates a specific, real subject's own traits for comic effect, while a stereotype flattens an entire group into a generic, assumed set of traits.
cards.n: Caricature is a deliberate technique writers can be praised for; calling writing stereotyped is usually a criticism, not a technique.

cards.q: Decide which satirical tool fits: a cartoon exaggerates a senator's already-large ears and nose to mock his vote.
cards.a: Caricature; the humor comes from exaggerating the senator's own physical features rather than imitating a text or attacking an institution generally.
cards.n: Caricature has to start from something real, so the analytic move is naming the trait exaggerated and the judgment it invites.

cards.q: Explain why a writer often subordinates the less important of two ideas rather than presenting them as separate sentences.
cards.a: Subordinating one idea signals to the reader which point is secondary, so the sentence argues for a hierarchy of importance instead of listing facts as equals.
cards.n: A string of equal simple sentences gives a reader no hierarchy, which is how choppy prose can be grammatically flawless and unpersuasive.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'Determined to finish before dark, the crew worked through the storm.'
cards.a: A participial phrase, 'Determined to finish before dark,' opening the sentence and front-loading the crew's motivation before naming their action.
cards.n: Don't confuse this with an absolute phrase; a participial phrase modifies the subject specifically, not the whole clause.

cards.q: Explain the effect of opening a sentence with a participial phrase rather than the subject.
cards.a: It delays the main subject and verb, forcing the reader to hold a condition or motive in mind before learning who acted, which can heighten suspense or foreground cause.
cards.n: The risk is a dangling modifier, since the phrase attaches to whatever subject follows and will attach to the wrong one if you let it.

cards.q: Contrast the rhetorical effect of a single absolute phrase versus a full subordinate clause conveying the same idea.
cards.a: An absolute phrase feels compressed and image-like, almost cinematic, while a subordinate clause with 'because' or 'as' makes the same relationship feel more logically explicit.
cards.n: Both can convey simultaneity or cause, but the absolute phrase reads as more literary and less argumentative.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields.'
cards.a: Anaphora; repeating 'we shall fight' at the start of each clause builds mounting resolve through accumulation.
cards.n: The repeated clause holds still while the place changes, so the sentence enacts the idea that ground may shift and resolve will not.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here.' (Gettysburg Address)
cards.a: Antithesis; contrasting 'say' and 'did' sets empty words against enduring action, undercutting the speech's own occasion to redirect focus to the soldiers.
cards.n: Lincoln's prediction turned out to be wrong, and that irony is standard material for the sophistication point on this speech.

cards.q: Apply an appositive to add a credential to this sentence: 'The engineer warned that the bridge was unsafe.'
cards.a: 'The engineer, a thirty-year veteran of municipal inspections, warned that the bridge was unsafe' - the appositive adds authority without a separate clause.
cards.h: → noun phrase, not a new clause
cards.n: An appositive works here because 'a thirty-year veteran' is a noun phrase, not a full clause with its own verb.

cards.q: Contrast 'which' and 'that' in formal written English.
cards.a: 'That' introduces a restrictive clause essential to identifying the noun and takes no comma; 'which' introduces a nonrestrictive clause adding extra, removable information and is set off by a comma.
cards.h: → essential, no comma vs extra, comma
cards.n: Misusing 'which' for a restrictive clause is one of the most common style errors AP readers notice, even though it rarely triggers a Row B penalty alone.

cards.q: Define a comma splice and give an example.
cards.a: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma with no coordinating conjunction, such as 'The evidence was strong, the jury still hesitated.' It should be a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a conjunction.
cards.h: → two sentences glued by just a comma
cards.n: Comma splices turn up constantly in revision-in-context items, where the credited fix is usually a semicolon or an added conjunction.
x: two sentences joined by only a comma

cards.q: Define a dangling modifier and give an example.
cards.a: A descriptive phrase placed so it appears to modify the wrong word, often because the word it should modify is missing, as in 'Having finished the report, the printer jammed,' where the printer did not finish the report.
cards.h: → modifier with no clear noun to attach to
cards.n: Dangling modifiers are common in rushed timed writing when a sentence gets restructured mid-thought.

cards.q: Contrast 'who' and 'whom' in formal usage.
cards.a: 'Who' is a subject pronoun, used when the pronoun performs the action, as in 'who wrote the letter.' 'Whom' is an object pronoun, used when the pronoun receives the action, as in 'to whom it may concern.'
cards.n: A quick test: if 'he' fits, use 'who'; if 'him' fits, use 'whom.'

cards.q: Define a misplaced modifier and give an example.
cards.a: A descriptive word or phrase positioned too far from the word it modifies, creating an unintended meaning, as in 'She almost drove her kids to school every day,' which suggests she rarely finished the drive rather than that she nearly did it daily.
cards.h: → modifier too far from its target word
cards.n: Reading the sentence and asking what word sits right next to the modifier usually catches the error fast.

cards.q: Explain the parallel structure error in 'The policy will reduce costs, improving morale, and it protects jobs.'
cards.a: The three items in a series should share the same grammatical form; mixing a base verb, a gerund, and a full clause breaks the parallelism. A corrected version reads 'reduce costs, improve morale, and protect jobs.'
cards.h: → match the grammatical form across a series
cards.n: Broken parallelism is easy to miss in a timed essay because each clause sounds fine read alone.

cards.q: Contrast a restrictive and a nonrestrictive clause.
cards.a: A restrictive clause narrows down which specific thing is meant and cannot be removed without changing the sentence's meaning. A nonrestrictive clause adds extra detail that could be deleted without changing which thing is meant.
cards.n: This same essential-vs-extra distinction underlies the which/that rule tested elsewhere in this unit.

cards.q: Explain why subject-verb agreement errors increase when a long prepositional phrase sits between the subject and the verb.
cards.a: A writer's ear tracks the noun closest to the verb rather than the true subject, producing errors like 'The list of items are long,' where 'list,' not 'items,' is the actual subject requiring a singular verb.
cards.h: → nearest noun, not the true subject, misleads the ear
cards.n: Cross out the prepositional phrase and reread what is left, since the sentence usually corrects itself once the noise is gone.

cards.q: Define malapropism and give an example.
cards.a: The mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding one, producing an unintentionally absurd meaning, as in saying someone is 'the pineapple of politeness' instead of 'pinnacle.'
cards.h: → wrong word, similar sound, absurd result
cards.n: A malapropism is an error within the world of the text; authors often put one in a character's mouth on purpose to reveal something about them.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'That lawyer is a real wolf in cheap clothing.'
cards.a: Malapropism - 'cheap' is mistakenly substituted for the similar-sounding 'sheep's,' replacing the intended idiom with an absurd, unintended meaning.
cards.n: Malapropisms are a favorite device for characterizing a pompous or careless speaker in satire.

cards.q: Define bombast and give an example.
cards.a: Pompous, overblown language that is far more elevated or dramatic than its subject deserves, such as calling a minor scheduling conflict 'an unprecedented catastrophe.'
cards.h: → inflated language for a small subject
cards.n: Bombast is a judgment rather than a neutral label, so calling a passage bombastic is already a criticism of the writer.

cards.q: Define vitriol and give an example.
cards.a: Harsh, bitterly critical language meant to wound or condemn, sharper and more personal in its hostility than ordinary criticism, such as branding an opponent's plan 'a con dressed up as compassion.'
cards.n: Vitriol and invective overlap; vitriol emphasizes bitterness, invective emphasizes direct verbal abuse.

cards.q: Define a vignette as a form of evidence in a passage.
cards.a: A brief, vivid scene or descriptive sketch used to illustrate a point through a single concentrated image rather than a fully developed narrative.
cards.h: → short vivid scene, not a full story
cards.n: A vignette differs from an anecdote in scale: an anecdote usually has a beginning, middle, and end; a vignette is closer to one frozen image.

cards.q: Contrast an anecdote and a vignette as forms of evidence.
cards.a: An anecdote is a brief story with a sequence of events leading to a point. A vignette is a single vivid scene or image with little to no narrative sequence, favoring atmosphere over plot.
cards.n: The test is whether anything changes: an anecdote turns on an event, while a vignette holds still and asks to be looked at.

cards.q: Define idiolect in style analysis.
cards.a: The distinctive, individual pattern of word choice, syntax, and speech habits unique to one speaker or writer, as opposed to the shared conventions of a whole dialect or era.
cards.h: → one writer's own signature pattern of language
cards.n: Analyzing a passage's idiolect matters most when a writer's individual voice, not any single device, is what drives the passage's effect.

cards.q: Explain how a sudden shift in register can function as a rhetorical choice within a passage.
cards.a: Dropping from formal, elevated diction into a blunt colloquial phrase, or the reverse, can jolt a reader's attention, signal sincerity breaking through formality, or mark a pivot in the writer's argument.
cards.n: Register shifts are easy to quote and easy to misdate, since a phrase that felt blunt in 1960 can read as neutral to a reader now.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The White House issued a statement denying the allegations.'
cards.a: Metonymy - 'the White House' substitutes for the president or presidential administration, a closely associated entity standing in for what it represents.
cards.n: Metonymy hides a choice here: naming the building instead of a person spreads responsibility across a whole institution.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'All hands were needed on deck before the storm hit.'
cards.a: Synecdoche - 'hands' stands in for the sailors as whole people, a part representing the whole.
cards.n: Synecdoche also runs the other way, whole for part: 'Germany beat Brazil' puts a nation in place of eleven players. Do not use 'Washington' for the government as the example — that is metonymy, an associated place standing in for an institution, like 'the White House'.

cards.q: Define a maxim and contrast it with an aphorism.
cards.a: A maxim is a short statement of practical wisdom meant as a guide to conduct, such as 'measure twice, cut once.' It differs from an aphorism mainly in emphasis: a maxim gives advice for action, while an aphorism states a general truth.
cards.n: Maxims usually arrive in the imperative, and that grammatical mood is the fastest tell that advice rather than observation is on offer.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'Fortune favors the bold.'
cards.a: An aphorism - a short, memorable statement expressing a general truth in a self-contained sentence.
cards.n: Proverb would also be defensible, since the line is traditional, but aphorism is the safer label for a printed AP passage.

cards.q: State the overall format of the AP English Language and Composition exam.
cards.a: Section I: 45 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes, worth 45% of the score. Section II: three free-response essays in 2 hours 15 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period), worth 55%.
cards.h: → two sections with times and weights
cards.n: Total testing time is 3 hours 15 minutes; the FRQs are worth more than the entire MC section.

cards.q: State what Section I of the AP Lang exam contains.
cards.a: 45 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes across five or so passages, split between reading questions (rhetorical analysis of nonfiction passages) and writing questions (revising a draft passage for argument, evidence, and style).
cards.n: Roughly 23-25 reading-analysis questions and 20-22 writing/revision questions - budget about 80 seconds per question.

cards.q: Contrast the two kinds of multiple-choice questions on the AP Lang exam.
cards.a: Reading questions ask what a published passage does - the writer's choices, purpose, audience, and reasoning. Writing questions present a student draft and ask which revision best achieves a stated goal, such as adding evidence or improving a transition.
cards.n: Writing questions always name a goal; the right answer is the one that serves that goal, not the prettiest sentence.

cards.q: State the structure of Section II of the AP Lang exam.
cards.a: Three essays in 2 hours 15 minutes: Q1 Synthesis, Q2 Rhetorical Analysis, Q3 Argument. The first 15 minutes are a suggested reading period for the synthesis source packet; each essay is then given about 40 minutes.
cards.n: The essays are equally weighted, so never let one essay eat another's time.

cards.q: Explain how to use the 15-minute reading period.
cards.a: Read the Q1 prompt first, decide a tentative position, then skim all sources marking each one's stance and one usable quotation. Sketch a three-part line of reasoning. You may begin writing before the 15 minutes end.
cards.n: Reading sources without a position first is the main way students burn the reading period.

cards.q: Identify what the synthesis question (Q1) demands.
cards.a: Take a defensible position on the issue and develop an argument that incorporates and cites at least three of six or seven provided sources as support. The sources are evidence for your claim, not the subject of the essay.
cards.n: The prompt's phrasing is usually 'develop a position' - a summary of the debate with no position cannot earn Row A.

cards.q: Identify what the rhetorical analysis question (Q2) demands.
cards.a: Read a nonfiction passage with a given rhetorical situation, then analyze the rhetorical choices the writer makes to achieve their purpose - explaining how and why the choices work on that audience, not merely which devices appear.
cards.n: The thesis must name the writer's message or purpose; a list of devices alone does not earn Row A.

cards.q: Identify what the argument question (Q3) demands.
cards.a: Respond to a short prompt or quotation by taking your own defensible position and supporting it with evidence you supply - personal experience, observation, reading, history, current events - developed with commentary.
cards.n: No passage is provided, so evidence quality is entirely on you; specific named examples beat general assertions.

cards.q: State the three rows of the AP Lang essay rubric and their point values.
cards.a: Row A: Thesis, 0-1 point. Row B: Evidence and Commentary, 0-4 points. Row C: Sophistication, 0-1 point. Total 6 points per essay.
cards.n: The same 6-point rubric applies to all three essays; Row B alone is two-thirds of the score.

cards.q: Explain exactly what earns the Row A thesis point.
cards.a: One point for a defensible thesis that responds to the prompt with a position, and that may preview the line of reasoning. It must be in the introduction or conclusion and be more than a restatement of the prompt.
cards.n: It is all-or-nothing: a partially defensible thesis earns zero, not a half point.

cards.q: Identify the most common reasons students lose the Row A point.
cards.a: Restating the prompt; describing the passage or sources instead of claiming; listing devices with no message ('the author uses ethos, pathos, and logos'); an obvious, undebatable statement; or a thesis buried mid-essay with nothing in the intro or conclusion.
cards.n: Write the thesis last in paragraph one, in one sentence, and make sure a reasonable person could disagree with it.

cards.q: Explain the Row B scale from 0 to 4.
cards.a: 0: no relevant evidence, or the response only restates the thesis. 1: mostly general evidence, and/or evidence summarized rather than explained. 2: some specific relevant evidence, with explanation of how some of it relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or the line of reasoning is faulty. 3: specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning, with explanation of how some of the evidence supports that line of reasoning. 4: specific evidence for all claims in a line of reasoning, with commentary that consistently explains how the evidence supports it.
cards.n: The jump from 1 to 2 is the jump from summarizing evidence to explaining it; the jump from 2 to 3 is establishing a real line of reasoning.

cards.q: Contrast a Row B score of 3 and a Row B score of 4.
cards.a: A 3 supports most claims with specific evidence and explains some of it. A 4 sustains it: every claim has specific, well-chosen evidence and the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports a coherent line of reasoning.
cards.n: Consistency and a visible line of reasoning are the difference; one brilliant paragraph among three thin ones is a 3.

cards.q: Explain what the Row C sophistication point rewards.
cards.a: One point for a response that demonstrates sophistication of thought or a complex understanding of the rhetorical situation, sustained across the essay rather than shown in a single sentence.
cards.n: Fewer than one in ten essays earns this point; it cannot be faked with grand-sounding closing lines.

cards.q: Identify the recognized routes to earning the sophistication point.
cards.a: Explaining the significance or implications of the argument in a broader context; explaining the tensions, contradictions, or nuances within the issue; consistently engaging the complexity of the rhetorical situation; or writing with a vivid, persuasive style that is consistently controlled.
cards.n: Choose one route and sustain it; attempting all four superficially reads as unfocused.

cards.q: Identify what does NOT earn the sophistication point.
cards.a: Sweeping generalizations ('humans have always struggled with this'), a single fancy sentence, unsupported claims about society, dense vocabulary without substance, and hedged both-sides commentary that never commits.
cards.n: Readers are told to reward sustained complexity, not isolated flourishes.

cards.q: State a workable timing plan for the AP Lang free-response section.
cards.a: 15 minutes reading and planning Q1; 40 minutes writing Q1; 5 minutes planning and 35 minutes writing Q2; 5 minutes planning and 30 minutes writing Q3; 5 minutes final check. Wear a watch and switch essays on schedule even if unfinished.
cards.n: Three complete decent essays outscore two excellent ones plus a fragment, because each is scored independently out of 6.

cards.q: Explain how to read a synthesis source set quickly.
cards.a: Read the prompt and take a position first. Then, for each source, read the header, the first and last paragraph, and skim the middle, jotting a two-word stance label and starring one usable line. Note which sources conflict - that tension is where sophistication lives.
cards.n: Charts and images count as sources and are underused; they often supply the cleanest data point.

cards.q: Explain how to write a rhetorical analysis body paragraph.
cards.a: Name the rhetorical choice; quote the specific evidence briefly; explain the effect on the intended audience; then link that effect to the writer's overall purpose. Choice, evidence, effect, purpose - in that order, every paragraph.
cards.n: The 'effect' and 'purpose' steps are the ones students skip, and they are exactly where Row B points live.

cards.q: Explain how to organize a rhetorical analysis essay other than device by device.
cards.a: Organize by the argument's movement: how the writer shifts from establishing credibility, to intensifying urgency, to demanding action - analyzing choices as they serve each stage. This foregrounds purpose instead of cataloguing techniques.
cards.n: Chunking the passage by rhetorical purpose is the surest structural route away from device-hunting.

cards.q: Identify why 'device-hunting' lowers a rhetorical analysis score.
cards.a: Naming devices without explaining their effect produces evidence with no commentary, capping Row B at 1 or 2. A correct label ('this is anaphora') proves nothing about how the passage works on its audience.
cards.n: You may earn a 6 without naming a single device by name, as long as you explain the choices.

cards.q: Identify why summarizing the passage or sources lowers a score.
cards.a: Summary reports content; the rubric rewards analysis of how content works. A summary-driven essay usually has no defensible thesis (Row A zero) and evidence without commentary (Row B 1-2).
cards.n: If your paragraph could be written by someone who agreed with nothing you believe, it is summary.

cards.q: Explain why five-paragraph autopilot hurts on AP Lang.
cards.a: The formula forces exactly three body paragraphs whether the argument needs two or five, encourages one-source-per-paragraph listing, and spends space on formulaic intros and restating conclusions instead of commentary. Let the line of reasoning set the paragraph count.
cards.n: There is no required number of paragraphs; readers score reasoning, not shape.

cards.q: Explain how to handle the argument essay's requirement to take a position.
cards.a: State one clear position in the thesis and hold it. You may qualify - agree with limits or under conditions - but you must be committed enough that a reader could argue against you; balanced 'both sides have points' essays fail Row A.
cards.n: Qualifying is not fence-sitting: 'X is justified only when Y' is a strong, defensible position.

cards.q: Define what an AP prompt means by 'evaluate.'
cards.a: To evaluate is to judge the merit, validity, or effectiveness of something against criteria and to argue for that judgment - not to describe or summarize it.
cards.n: Evaluate prompts require stated criteria, since a judgment with no standard behind it is an opinion rather than an argument.

cards.q: Explain the 'defend, challenge, or qualify' instruction on an AP Lang prompt.
cards.a: Defend means argue the claim is right; challenge means argue it is wrong; qualify means agree in part while specifying the conditions or limits under which it holds. You must choose one and sustain it - all three are equally scoreable.
cards.n: Qualify is usually the most defensible choice because it lets you use counterevidence as support.

cards.q: Explain how to write a strong qualified position.
cards.a: Name what you accept in the claim, name the conditions or cases where it fails, and state the principle that separates them. 'Civil disobedience is justified when legal channels have been exhausted, but not when the cause has not yet been argued publicly.'
cards.n: A qualified thesis must still be one sentence with one governing position, not two claims joined by 'but.'

cards.q: Explain how to use the context paragraph that precedes an FRQ passage.
cards.a: It supplies the rhetorical situation - writer, audience, occasion, exigence, and purpose - which the analysis must use. Mining it for audience and occasion is the fastest way to make commentary specific rather than generic.
cards.h: → what it gives + how to use
cards.n: Ignoring the framing paragraph is a common cause of vague, audience-free commentary on Q2.

cards.q: Explain what a Q2 rhetorical analysis thesis must contain.
cards.a: It must state the writer's purpose or message and indicate the kinds of choices used to achieve it, in a way that can be developed - not a list of devices and not a summary of the passage's topic.
cards.n: 'Uses ethos, pathos, and logos to persuade the audience' is the classic Row A zero.

cards.q: Explain what a Q1 synthesis thesis must contain.
cards.a: It must state your own defensible position on the prompt's issue, specific enough to be argued with the sources, and it should suggest the reasoning that will organize the essay. It should not simply report what the sources collectively say.
cards.n: A thesis that only reports the debate cannot be argued with, and reporting is the most common way Row A gets lost on Q1.

cards.q: Explain what counts as acceptable evidence on the Q3 argument essay.
cards.a: Anything specific and accurate: history, current events, literature, film, science, personal experience, or observation. Readers do not privilege one domain; they reward specificity, accuracy, and the commentary that connects it to the claim.
cards.n: Two developed examples with real commentary beat five name-dropped ones.

cards.q: Explain the ratio of evidence to commentary you should aim for.
cards.a: Roughly one sentence of evidence to two of commentary. If a paragraph is mostly quotation or mostly source summary, it is under-analyzed no matter how apt the evidence is.
cards.n: Highlight your quotations: if more than a third of a body paragraph is highlighted, cut evidence and add commentary.

cards.q: State a 5-minute end-of-essay checklist.
cards.a: Does the thesis take a defensible position? Does each topic sentence make a claim? Is every quotation followed by explanation? Are at least three sources cited (Q1)? Does the last sentence of each paragraph tie back to the thesis?
cards.n: Most of these are cheaper to handle while drafting than at the end, so treat the list as habits rather than a final sweep.

cards.q: Explain the best strategy for AP Lang multiple-choice reading questions.
cards.a: Read the question stem before rereading the lines, return to the cited lines and their surrounding context, predict an answer in your own words, then find the choice closest to it. Eliminate choices that are true of the passage but do not answer the stem.
cards.n: The most common wrong answer is accurate about the passage but irrelevant to what the question asked.

cards.q: Explain the best strategy for AP Lang multiple-choice writing/revision questions.
cards.a: Identify the stated goal in the stem (add evidence, sharpen the claim, improve the transition), then judge each option only against that goal. Read the sentences before and after the insertion point, since the answer usually depends on that link.
cards.n: Grammatically fine but goal-irrelevant options are the standard distractors here.

cards.q: State the guessing policy and pacing target for the multiple-choice section.
cards.a: There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. With 45 questions in 60 minutes, the pace is about 80 seconds per question, or roughly 11-12 minutes per passage set.
cards.n: Never leave a blank; mark and return rather than stalling on one hard question.

cards.q: Explain how to annotate a passage efficiently during the exam.
cards.a: The exam is fully digital in Bluebook, so annotate with the app's highlight and note tools rather than a pen: highlight the shifts (but, yet, however), the audience and occasion clues, and one or two places where tone changes, and drop a short note where each purpose-driven chunk of the passage begins. Do not highlight every device you recognize.
cards.h: → what to mark + what to skip
cards.n: Annotation should produce a structure you can write from, not a decorated page.

cards.q: State how AP Lang exam scores are reported and composed.
cards.a: The final AP score is a 1-5 scale. It combines the multiple-choice section (45%) with the three free-response essays (55%), each essay scored 0-6 on the same rubric and weighted equally.
cards.n: A composite around half the available points typically reaches a 3; exact cut scores shift each year.

cards.q: Explain how AP readers score the essays.
cards.a: Each essay is scored row by row against the 6-point analytic rubric by a trained reader, independently of your other essays, and readers are instructed to reward what the response does well rather than deduct for what is missing.
cards.n: There is no penalty carried across essays: a weak Q1 does not lower your Q2 score.

cards.q: Explain how grammar and mechanics affect an AP Lang essay score.
cards.a: There is no separate grammar row. Errors matter only when they interfere with the reader's understanding of the argument; a well-reasoned essay with imperfect surface polish can still earn 6.
cards.n: This is not license to ignore clarity - unreadable sentences do cost points through Row B.

cards.q: Explain what happens if an essay does not respond to the prompt.
cards.a: Responses that are off-topic, that only repeat the prompt, or that are written in a language other than English receive a score of 0. A blank or completely blank-page response receives no score at all.
cards.n: These outcomes are rare but absolute, and the most common route to one is answering a prompt that was skimmed rather than read.

cards.q: Decide what to do when you have 10 minutes left and no essay started on Q3.
cards.a: Write a one-sentence defensible thesis immediately, then two body paragraphs with one specific example each and two sentences of commentary each. Skip the introduction beyond the thesis and skip the conclusion. Thesis plus real commentary can still earn 3-4 points.
cards.n: A thesis with two developed paragraphs scores far above a polished intro with nothing after it.

cards.q: Explain how to plan an essay in five minutes.
cards.a: Write the thesis in one sentence, then list two to four subclaims in the order they build, and note the single piece of evidence attached to each. That list is your topic sentences; if the subclaims do not build, reorder before writing.
cards.n: Reordering costs seconds on a list and minutes once paragraphs exist, which is the whole reason to write the list first.

cards.q: Identify habits that make commentary generic.
cards.a: Naming the audience as 'the reader' rather than the specific audience; explaining that a choice makes the argument 'more effective' or 'more persuasive' without saying how; and repeating the thesis instead of advancing it.
cards.n: Replace 'this is effective' with 'this makes a skeptical legislator feel the cost personally.'

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang MC question asking the function of a sentence or paragraph.
cards.a: Read the sentence in its surrounding context and ask what job it does for the argument - introduces a counterargument, provides an example, signals a shift, draws a conclusion - then choose the option naming that job.
cards.n: Function questions ask what a sentence does rather than what it says, so a choice that accurately paraphrases the content is often a trap.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang MC question asking the effect of a specific word or phrase.
cards.a: Identify the word's connotation and what it implies about the writer's attitude toward the subject, then match that implication to the answer choice, eliminating options that describe the word accurately but miss its effect.
cards.n: These items reward the attitude behind the word, so separate denotation, which any dictionary supplies, from what the choice implies.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang MC question about the relationship between two paragraphs.
cards.a: Name the logical move in your own words first - does the second paragraph exemplify, complicate, extend, or refute the first - then pick the answer choice matching that relationship.
cards.n: Naming it yourself first is the whole point, since reading the options first lets the test writer's wording pull you off course.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang MC question that asks you to identify a shift.
cards.a: Scan for markers - but, yet, however, a change in verb tense, a new pronoun, a sudden short sentence - locate the exact line where the shift occurs, then choose the answer naming both what changes and its direction.
cards.n: Choices that name the change but reverse its direction are common here, so check which side of the shift each half describes.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang writing/revision question that asks which choice best adds evidence.
cards.a: Check the stated goal in the stem first, then test each option against the paragraph's existing claim: eliminate any choice that is off-topic, repeats a point already made, or is evidence with no clear link to that claim.
cards.n: Interesting but unrelated material is the standard distractor, because relevance is harder to judge quickly than plausibility.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang writing/revision question that asks which choice best combines two sentences.
cards.a: Look for the option that subordinates the less important idea into a dependent clause or modifier while keeping the more important idea in the independent clause, preserving the original meaning.
cards.n: Watch for combinations that are grammatical but shift the emphasis, since preserving the original meaning is part of what is scored.

cards.q: Explain the AP Lang MC 'EXCEPT' or 'NOT' question format and how to work it.
cards.a: The stem asks for the one choice that does NOT fit a stated pattern, so three of the four choices will be true and one false; work through options normally, tracking which you have confirmed true, and select the one left unconfirmed.
cards.n: Misreading EXCEPT and picking the first true answer is one of the most common careless MC errors.

cards.q: Explain whether a strong Row A thesis guarantees any Row B points.
cards.a: No. The rows are scored independently: an essay can earn the thesis point with a clear, defensible claim and still score low on Row B if the body paragraphs lack specific evidence or sustained commentary tied to a line of reasoning.
cards.n: Students sometimes over-invest in a polished thesis and under-invest in the body, where four of six points live.

cards.q: Contrast qualifying a claim and hedging (fence-sitting) on the AP Lang argument essay.
cards.a: Qualifying names specific conditions under which a position holds, committing to a precise, defensible claim; hedging avoids commitment altogether by presenting both sides as equally valid with no stance taken, which fails Row A.
cards.n: The tell is whether the sentence could be disagreed with, since a real qualifier still leaves something for an opponent to attack.

cards.q: Explain whether a longer essay automatically scores higher on the AP Lang rubric.
cards.a: No. The rubric rewards specific evidence, sustained commentary, and a coherent line of reasoning, not word count; a shorter, tightly developed essay outscores a longer one padded with summary or repetition.
cards.n: Length correlates with score only because developed essays run longer, and padding reverses that relationship entirely.

cards.q: Explain a fast brainstorming technique for choosing Q3 argument evidence under time pressure.
cards.a: Scan two mental buckets - lived or observed experience, and public knowledge such as history, current events, or reading - and grab the first specific, nameable example from each; a concrete detail beats a vague claim you cannot support.
cards.n: Name the example rather than gesturing at a category, since one specific case from either bucket outscores a general claim about both.

cards.q: Explain the expected length and development of an AP Lang FRQ response.
cards.a: There is no minimum word count or page requirement; readers score the quality of the thesis, evidence, and commentary, not length. Fully developed essays with a real line of reasoning tend to run long, but padding does not help.
cards.n: Handwriting speed is not scored, so an essay that runs shorter because it was planned is not at a disadvantage against a sprawling one.

cards.q: Explain what the context note before each Section I passage typically provides.
cards.a: A brief framing statement giving the source, author, approximate date, and situation - enough of the rhetorical situation to identify audience and occasion without reading the full passage first.
cards.n: Skipping it costs more than the seconds it saves, because MC questions about audience and purpose are often answerable from it alone.

cards.q: Explain how to handle a Q2 passage whose intended audience shifts partway through.
cards.a: Treat the shift itself as a rhetorical choice worth analyzing: identify where the address changes, such as from the general public to policymakers directly, and explain what that pivot allows that a single audience would not.
cards.n: Passages with a divided audience usually have a headnote naming both, so the shift is signposted before the passage even begins.

cards.q: Explain how to handle an AP Lang argument prompt built on a metaphorical or figurative quotation.
cards.a: Translate the figurative language into a literal, arguable claim before drafting a thesis - state in plain terms what the metaphor asserts about human behavior or society - so your argument responds to that claim.
cards.n: Essays that never unpack the metaphor tend to drift into paraphrase instead of argument.

cards.q: Explain whether AP Lang FRQs must be written in the printed order.
cards.a: No. You may write the three essays in any order within the 2 hour 15 minute block; the 15-minute period is designated reading time for the Q1 sources, but a student stronger elsewhere may start with Q2 or Q3 instead.
cards.n: Time is not divided for you inside the block, so leaving one essay with ten minutes is a self-inflicted problem rather than a rule.

cards.q: Explain how to use line references in AP Lang MC question stems efficiently.
cards.a: Locate the cited line numbers in the margin, then read a few lines before and after rather than the single line alone, since the correct answer usually depends on context the isolated line does not supply.
cards.n: Reading only the cited line is the fastest way into a distractor, because effect nearly always depends on what surrounds it.

cards.q: Explain a triage plan for Q1 or Q2 when time is running out mid-essay.
cards.a: Stop drafting new paragraphs and write a clear final sentence for the paragraph in progress, then use remaining minutes for one concise concluding statement that names the stakes, rather than starting a point you cannot finish.
cards.n: An unfinished paragraph with no landing sentence reads as more disorganized than a shorter, complete essay.

cards.q: Explain the benefit of preparing a flexible thesis template before exam day.
cards.a: A reusable frame, such as naming a position, listing supporting grounds, and acknowledging a limit, lets you draft a defensible, roadmap thesis quickly under time pressure without inventing sentence structure for each new prompt.
cards.n: A template turns into a liability when the same phrasing is reused word for word, since a reader can see a slot that was never filled.

cards.q: Explain the AP Lang rubric's holistic scoring principle within Row B.
cards.a: Readers weigh the essay's evidence and commentary as a whole rather than checking off a fixed list of required moves; two essays with different structures can both reach a 4 if each sustains specific evidence and consistent explanation.
cards.n: Holistic also means one weak paragraph does not sink an otherwise strong essay, so a shaky middle section is not worth panicking over.

cards.q: Explain how to answer an AP Lang MC question about a chart, graph, or image embedded in a passage.
cards.a: Read the title, axis labels, or caption first to establish what is being measured, then treat the visual as an argument with its own claim, asking what choice in its design shapes how a viewer reads it.
cards.n: Design choices such as a truncated axis or a hand-picked date range are fair game, and they carry the visual's real argument.

cards.q: Explain the risk of overquoting a Q2 passage instead of quoting selectively.
cards.a: Copying long stretches of the passage leaves little room to explain any of it, so the paragraph reads as evidence with thin commentary; a few precise words analyzed closely earn more Row B credit than a long, under-analyzed quotation.
cards.n: Three or four quoted words are usually plenty, and quoting less leaves more of the paragraph for the explanation that actually scores.

cards.q: Explain how AP readers are trained to stay consistent across thousands of essays (norming).
cards.a: Before scoring, readers practice on sample essays already scored by table leaders, discussing borderline cases until their judgments align, which is why the same rubric language produces consistent scores across many readers.
cards.n: Norming is also why guessing at what a particular reader might personally like is wasted effort; the rubric language is the standard.

cards.q: Explain how to choose a position on an AP Lang argument prompt when you have no strong personal opinion.
cards.a: Pick the side you can support with the most specific, concrete evidence, not necessarily the side you believe most strongly - the rubric rewards a well-argued defensible position, not sincerity.
cards.n: Readers cannot tell what you actually believe, and an essay arguing a position you hold weakly reads just like one you hold firmly.

cards.q: Explain why an AP Lang MC answer choice containing 'always' or 'never' is often wrong even when it sounds plausible.
cards.a: Absolute words claim something holds in every case, and passages rarely support a claim that strong, so readers should test extreme-language choices against the text before picking them.
cards.h: → absolute language rarely matches nuanced text
cards.n: This is a useful first filter, not an absolute rule; occasionally an extreme-language choice is correct, so still check it against the text.

cards.q: Define a half-right answer trap on the AP Lang multiple-choice section.
cards.a: A choice that correctly names a device or idea in the passage but pairs it with the wrong effect, location, or explanation, making it attractive but incorrect.
cards.n: These traps are common because eliminating an answer that's 'almost right' feels riskier than picking one that's 'somewhat right.'

cards.q: Explain how to catch a half-right answer trap before selecting it.
cards.a: Check every clause of the answer choice against the passage, not just the part that sounds familiar, since test-writers often build the trap into the second half of the sentence.
cards.n: A choice can be true for the first ten words and false for the last five; read the whole thing.

cards.q: Identify why an answer choice that is technically true about the passage can still be wrong on an AP Lang MC question.
cards.a: Because it does not answer the actual question being asked - it may be true but irrelevant to the specific function, effect, or relationship the stem asks about.
cards.n: Reread the stem before committing, since the question rather than the passage decides which true statement counts as the answer.

cards.q: Explain the trap in an overly narrow AP Lang MC answer choice.
cards.a: A choice can describe only one small detail from the passage instead of the broader function or effect the question actually asks about, making it too limited to be the best answer.
cards.n: A narrow choice can still be literally true about the passage, which is exactly what makes it tempting.

cards.q: Explain the trap in an overly broad AP Lang MC answer choice.
cards.a: A choice can make a sweeping claim about the whole passage's purpose when the question only asks about a single sentence or paragraph's specific function.
cards.n: Broad and narrow traps are mirror images, so match the scope of the choice to the scope named in the stem before judging content.

cards.q: Decide what to do when two AP Lang MC choices both seem partly supported by the passage.
cards.a: Reread the question stem itself and pick whichever choice answers exactly what was asked, since one choice usually addresses the stem precisely and the other only adjacently.
cards.h: → match the choice to the stem
cards.n: Resist re-skimming the whole passage first; the stem itself usually narrows the choice faster than a fresh read.

cards.q: Identify the trap when an AP Lang MC choice states close to the exact opposite of the passage's actual effect.
cards.a: An opposite-effect distractor; it often reuses accurate vocabulary from the passage but reverses the direction of the effect, so skimming can mistake familiarity for correctness.
cards.n: Direction is the thing to verify: praise or criticism, increase or decrease, endorsement or rejection all flip easily under a skim.

cards.q: State a workable time split for planning versus writing a single 40-minute AP Lang FRQ.
cards.a: Roughly 5 to 8 minutes planning and annotating, with the remaining 32 to 35 minutes writing, leaving a couple of minutes to proofread if time allows.
cards.n: Longer, denser passages may justify a minute or two more planning time, borrowed from the writing minutes rather than added on top.

cards.q: Explain why spending too little time planning a Q3 argument essay tends to hurt the score more than it seems to save time.
cards.a: Without a planned line of reasoning, body paragraphs tend to drift or repeat the same point, which costs Row B points that planning would have protected.
cards.n: Five minutes of planning buys back more than five minutes of drafting, because a drifting paragraph cannot be rewritten in ink.

cards.q: Explain a fast way to select which sources to use first when planning the Q1 synthesis essay under time pressure.
cards.a: Skim each source for one sentence that could serve as a claim or a strong quotation, then group sources that agree or disagree with each other, since paired sources plan faster.
cards.n: This grouping step also gives the essay's line of reasoning a built-in structure before a single sentence is drafted.

cards.q: Decide which three sources to lead with when six are available and only 40 minutes remain: the two that agree, or two that clash plus one that complicates both.
cards.a: Two that clash plus one that complicates both; sources in tension give a line of reasoning more to analyze than sources that simply agree with each other.
cards.n: Agreement leaves a paragraph nothing to explain, while tension hands the essay a question it can visibly work through.

cards.q: Decide the sophistication move: an essay's conclusion explains a specific real-world limit on when the thesis would not hold. Does this likely earn the point?
cards.a: Likely yes; naming a specific situation where the argument's logic breaks down shows genuine complexity, one of the recognized paths to the sophistication point.
cards.h: → names a real limit or exception
cards.n: This move works because it shows the writer understands the argument's boundaries, not just its strongest case.

cards.q: Decide the sophistication move: an essay repeats 'furthermore' and 'moreover' but never adds a new layer of reasoning. Does this earn the point?
cards.a: Likely no; transition words alone are not complexity, and readers are trained to look past vocabulary for genuine additional reasoning.
cards.n: The same holds for elevated vocabulary, since the Row C point is earned by what the reasoning does and not by how sentences sound.

cards.q: Explain why explicitly writing 'this shows sophistication' in an essay does not earn the sophistication point.
cards.a: The point rewards the reasoning actually demonstrated in the writing, not a label claiming credit for it; readers score what the analysis does, not what it announces about itself.
cards.n: The same principle applies to writing 'this is a strong counterargument'; naming a move is not the same as making it.

cards.q: Apply a sophistication move to strengthen this flat claim: 'Social media harms teenagers.' Add one qualifying layer.
cards.a: 'Social media harms teenagers most acutely when parental oversight and offline friendships are both weak,' which adds a specific condition instead of a blanket claim.
cards.n: The qualifier narrows the claim without weakening it, which is exactly the difference between qualifying and backing away from a position.

cards.q: Explain the risk of choosing evidence for a Q3 argument essay based only on which example is most dramatic.
cards.a: A dramatic example that does not actually match the claim's logic can weaken the line of reasoning even while it entertains, so relevance should outweigh drama when choosing evidence.
cards.n: A less dramatic but tightly relevant example almost always outscores a vivid one that only loosely fits the claim.

cards.q: Decide the stronger evidence for a claim about school start times: one friend's tired mornings, or a cited study comparing two districts' start times.
cards.a: The cited study; it offers a comparison across a real sample, while the anecdote is a single case that cannot rule out other explanations.
cards.n: Personal experience is still legitimate Q3 evidence, but it works best as illustration beside a broader claim rather than as the whole case.

cards.q: Explain how a flexible thesis template can still earn the sophistication point rather than just the thesis point.
cards.a: A template that builds in a qualifying clause or an acknowledgment of complexity from the start gives the writer a head start on sophistication, as long as the content is not generic.
cards.n: A template only helps if the writer still fills it with the specific complexity of that prompt, not a phrase reused every time.

cards.q: Decide what to prioritize with 3 minutes left and one body paragraph unfinished: adding a new example, or writing a one-sentence link back to the thesis.
cards.a: The link back to the thesis; an unfinished paragraph that at least states its point and ties to the thesis reads as more complete than one left as a dangling example.
cards.n: Readers score what a paragraph accomplishes, and an unexplained example accomplishes nothing however good the example is.

cards.q: Explain how to decide which of the three FRQs to write first when none feels obviously easiest.
cards.a: Start with the essay whose sources or prompt you understood fastest on the first read, since early momentum on a clear plan matters more than tackling essays in printed order.
cards.n: Writing the clearest essay first also builds momentum and confidence for the harder two that follow.

cards.q: Explain why a distractor that repeats a passage's exact vocabulary is not automatically the correct answer.
cards.a: Test-writers often lift real words from the passage into wrong choices precisely because familiar language feels safe, so the words must still match the question's actual claim.
cards.h: → familiar wording is not proof of correctness
cards.n: The credited answer often paraphrases rather than quotes, so unfamiliar wording is never a reason to eliminate a choice.

cards.q: Decide whether this earns the Row A thesis point: 'Social media has both benefits and drawbacks for teenagers.'
cards.a: No; the statement lists two sides without taking a defensible position, so it reads as a topic restatement rather than a claim a reader could argue against.
cards.n: Adding one clause that commits to a side, even a qualified one, would likely fix this thesis without much rewriting.

cards.q: Decide whether this earns the Row A point: 'Because it erodes attention faster than it builds connection, social media harms teens more than it helps.'
cards.a: Yes; it takes a defensible position and previews the reasoning, attention versus connection, the essay will use to support it.
cards.n: The because clause is what lifts it past a bare position, since it names the reasoning the body paragraphs now have to deliver.

cards.q: Explain why writing out a full topic sentence during planning, rather than just a keyword, saves time later.
cards.a: A full topic sentence forces the line of reasoning to be decided during planning, so the writer is not improvising the paragraph's actual claim mid-draft.
cards.n: A one-word plan like 'ethos' still leaves the actual claim to be invented under pressure mid-paragraph.

cards.q: Explain the difference in what an AP Lang prompt asks for when it says 'evaluate the extent to which' versus a straightforward 'argue.'
cards.a: 'Evaluate the extent to which' expects the essay to weigh how much the claim holds true, inviting a qualified position, while a plain 'argue' prompt leaves the degree of agreement more open.
cards.n: Extent prompts practically invite a qualified thesis, and words like largely or only when signal the degree a reader is looking for.

cards.q: Decide how to spend an extra 2 minutes found at the end of the reading period: rereading a source, or outlining the thesis.
cards.a: Outlining the thesis; a written thesis and rough plan protect against losing the line of reasoning once writing begins, which matters more than one more pass over a source.
cards.n: A plan that exists only in the writer's head is easy to lose once the pressure of drafting begins.

cards.q: Explain why process-of-elimination works better than searching for the 'obviously right' choice on tricky AP Lang MC questions.
cards.a: Eliminating choices that are clearly false, off-topic, or too extreme narrows the field even when no option feels perfect, which is common on inference-heavy questions.
cards.n: Elimination also leaves you with a reason for the answer, which matters most on inference items where nothing feels obviously right.

cards.q: Explain why rereading only the topic sentence of each body paragraph is a fast way to check an essay's line of reasoning before time runs out.
cards.a: If the topic sentences alone tell a coherent story of the argument's progression, the line of reasoning likely holds; if they repeat each other, the essay is probably circling one point.
cards.n: This same check works even faster if the topic sentences were written out fully during planning rather than left as fragments.

cards.q: Explain why the context note before a Q2 or Q3 passage should shape your annotation before you start writing.
cards.a: It signals the speaker, occasion, and audience the readers already expect you to use, so annotating with that lens from the first read saves time re-reading for it later.
cards.n: Reading it twice, once before the passage and again before writing, is the cheapest way to keep a thesis anchored in the situation.

cards.q: Decide the flaw: the passage's metaphor undercuts the speaker's optimism, but an answer choice claims it reflects the speaker's nostalgia instead.
cards.a: A half-right trap; the choice correctly spots the metaphor but assigns it the wrong effect, so it fails even though it names a real device in the passage.
cards.n: The passage detail has to be checked against both halves of the choice, not just the noun it names.

cards.q: Explain why AP Lang essay scores from a student's three FRQs are summed rather than averaged before weighting.
cards.a: Each of the three essays earns its own 0-6 score independently against the rubric; these three scores are summed and then combined with the multiple-choice score according to the section weights to form the composite.
cards.n: Summing means each essay counts equally, so a strong Q3 can offset a weak Q1 instead of being diluted inside an average.

cards.q: Define an analytic (row-based) scoring model and contrast it with holistic scoring.
cards.a: Analytic scoring awards points row by row against fixed, named criteria, as the AP Lang essay rubric does. Holistic scoring assigns one overall impression score without breaking the judgment into separate criteria.
cards.h: → row-by-row criteria vs one overall impression
cards.n: Even though the overall rubric is analytic, Row B itself is scored holistically within its own 0-4 scale.

cards.q: Explain why an essay that only partly addresses a multi-part AP Lang prompt can still score well.
cards.a: Row A and Row B credit is earned by what the response does well against the rubric criteria, so a response that fully addresses most of the prompt with strong evidence and commentary can still earn most available points.
cards.n: This does not apply if the ignored part is the entire task, such as never taking a position on an argument prompt.

cards.q: Contrast how length and how quality separately affect an AP Lang essay score.
cards.a: Length alone earns no credit; a short, well-developed essay can outscore a long, repetitive one. Quality, meaning specific evidence and analytical commentary, is what the rubric rewards.
cards.n: The confusion persists because developed essays do run longer, but length is a symptom of development and never a cause of the score.

cards.q: Define the attribution line before each AP Lang Section I passage.
cards.a: A brief note giving the passage's author, title, date, and original context, which orients the rhetorical situation before you read a single sentence of the passage itself.
cards.n: The date matters most: a 1963 speech and a 2013 essay on the same subject face completely different audience assumptions.

cards.q: Explain why every passage on the AP Lang exam is nonfiction.
cards.a: The course tests rhetorical analysis of real arguments and information, not literary interpretation of fiction, so every reading and writing passage is drawn from nonfiction genres such as speeches, essays, and articles.
cards.n: This distinguishes AP Lang from AP Literature, which is built around fiction and poetry.

cards.q: State roughly how many passages Section I of the AP Lang exam is built around.
cards.a: About five passages, split between reading-focused sets analyzing a published nonfiction text and writing-focused sets asking you to revise a student draft.
cards.n: The exact number can vary slightly by form, so treat five as a planning estimate, not a fixed count.

cards.q: Explain what changes about your reading approach for a writing/revision passage compared to a reading passage in Section I.
cards.a: A writing passage is a student's draft, not a polished professional text, so you read it looking for what could be improved to meet a stated goal, rather than analyzing why an already-effective choice works.
cards.n: The stem always names the writer's goal, and a revision that improves the sentence but misses that goal is still the wrong choice.

cards.q: Explain what the standard Q2 instruction to 'analyze the rhetorical choices the writer makes' is directing you to do with your evidence.
cards.a: It signals that your job is to select specific choices, such as diction, syntax, or structure, and explain how each one serves the writer's purpose, rather than paraphrasing the passage's content or judging its argument.
cards.h: → what to select, what to explain
cards.n: Agreeing or disagreeing with the passage is the misread this instruction exists to prevent, and it costs Row B heavily.

cards.q: Contrast an AP Lang argument prompt that provides a specific quotation to respond to and one that poses an open question.
cards.a: A quotation prompt requires you to take a position on that exact claim, using its own key terms in your thesis. An open-question prompt gives more latitude to define the issue yourself, but still needs one clear, defensible position.
cards.n: Either type still requires one clear, defensible position - the prompt style changes your entry point, not the requirement.

cards.q: Explain the mistake of treating an AP Lang argument prompt as an invitation to write a personal narrative.
cards.a: The prompt asks for a defensible claim developed with evidence and reasoning, not a story about your own experience for its own sake; personal experience may serve as one piece of evidence, but it cannot replace an argument.
cards.n: A personal anecdote can open a body paragraph, but the paragraph still needs a claim and commentary, not just narration.

cards.q: Define what an AP Lang prompt means by a writer's 'rhetorical choices.'
cards.a: The deliberate decisions a writer makes in language and structure, such as word choice, sentence length and type, organization, appeals, and evidence, selected to achieve a specific effect on a specific audience.
cards.h: → deliberate decisions in language and structure
cards.n: This phrase appears in nearly every Q2 prompt verbatim, so it is worth having a ready checklist of choice categories.

cards.q: Decide the flaw: a Q3 argument essay never states the prompt's key term, 'civic duty,' anywhere in the thesis.
cards.a: The thesis fails to engage the prompt's actual terms, risking a reader's judgment that the essay argues a related but different claim rather than the one the prompt asked.
cards.n: Borrowing the prompt's key term is not the same as restating the prompt, and defining that term can itself become the argument.

cards.q: Contrast whose argument a Q2 rhetorical analysis thesis makes and whose argument a Q3 argument essay thesis makes.
cards.a: A Q2 thesis argues about the writer's purpose and choices in someone else's text. A Q3 thesis argues the student's own position on the prompt's issue, developed with the student's own evidence.
cards.h: → analyzing another writer's argument vs making your own
cards.n: Confusing the two shows up as a Q2 essay that agrees or disagrees with the passage instead of analyzing how the passage works.

cards.q: Explain why a Q2 passage is always provided in full while a Q3 argument essay is given no source passage at all.
cards.a: Q2 tests the ability to analyze an existing text's rhetorical choices, which requires that text to be present. Q3 tests the ability to construct an original argument from the student's own knowledge, so no passage is supplied.
cards.n: This is also why Q3 evidence must come from the student's own knowledge rather than close reading of a text.

cards.q: Explain what kind of source material typically makes up the Q1 synthesis source set.
cards.a: A mix of about six or seven sources in varied formats, such as prose articles, an image or cartoon, and a chart or graph, representing a range of perspectives on one debatable issue.
cards.n: The range of views is deliberate, since a set where every source agreed would leave a writer nothing to put in conversation.

cards.q: Decide which FRQ is being described: the response must incorporate at least three outside sources into an original argument.
cards.a: Q1, the synthesis question - it is the only FRQ that requires citing a minimum number of provided sources as support for a position.
cards.n: Q2 and Q3 never require a minimum source count, since neither is built around a provided source set.

cards.q: Explain why rereading the Q2 passage's attribution line before drafting a thesis can prevent a common scoring mistake.
cards.a: The attribution line often names the speaker, occasion, and audience; missing it can lead to a thesis that misidentifies the rhetorical situation, which weakens every claim about purpose built on top of it.
cards.n: A misread situation is hard to recover from, because every later sentence about purpose inherits the original mistake.

cards.q: Explain whether an essay with no thesis statement anywhere can still earn Row B evidence and commentary points.
cards.a: Yes - Row A and Row B are scored independently. An essay that develops a defensible line of reasoning with strong evidence and commentary can earn substantial Row B credit even without a clean, isolable thesis.
cards.n: Never skip attempting a thesis, but losing the Row A point alone does not cap the rest of the essay.

cards.q: Define what a 'defensible' thesis means for the Row A point.
cards.a: A thesis making a claim a reasonable reader could disagree with, supported by reasoning rather than an obvious fact, a personal preference, or a claim beyond what the prompt or passage can support.
cards.h: → a claim someone could reasonably contest
cards.n: A thesis can be debatable and still be wrong to argue if the passage or sources cannot actually support it.

cards.q: Identify the rubric row a body paragraph with rich evidence but generic, repetitive commentary would lose the most credit on.
cards.a: Row B - evidence alone does not earn full credit; the commentary explaining how that evidence supports the line of reasoning is what the row is actually weighted toward.
cards.n: Commentary that would fit any passage is the usual culprit, so tie every sentence to the specific evidence just quoted.

cards.q: Explain why the AP Lang rubric rewards a thesis that is 'defensible' rather than one that is 'correct.'
cards.a: The rubric does not judge whether the reader agrees with the position, only whether the position is arguable and supportable; a well-reasoned essay defending an unpopular claim can score as high as one defending a popular claim.
cards.n: This is why the safe-looking middle position is risky: agreeable is not the same as defensible, and vagueness fails Row A.

cards.q: Define rhetorical choice.
cards.a: Any deliberate decision a writer makes (a word, a structure, an appeal, an omission) understood as selected in order to affect a specific audience for a specific purpose.
cards.n: Say chooses, not uses. The verb choose forces you to explain why, which is where the points are.

cards.q: Contrast identifying a strategy and explaining its effect.
cards.a: Identifying names the device (the speaker uses anaphora); explaining effect states what the choice does to the audience and how it advances the purpose (the repetition builds momentum that makes inaction feel indefensible).
cards.n: The AP rubric rewards effect, not labels. A device list with no effect stalls at the low end of Row B.

cards.q: Explain what a line of reasoning is in a rhetorical analysis essay.
cards.a: The sequence of claims about the writer's choices that, taken in order, supports the thesis. Each paragraph advances the argument about purpose rather than walking through the passage device by device.
cards.n: Chronological device-hunting is the most common Q2 failure; organize by the argument, not by the passage.

cards.q: Contrast commentary and summary in a rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: Summary restates what the text says; commentary explains why the writer made a choice and what it accomplishes with the audience. Only commentary earns Row B credit.
cards.n: Test: if a reader who never saw the passage learns only its content from your sentence, it is summary.

cards.q: State what makes a thesis defensible on the rhetorical analysis question.
cards.a: It must make an arguable claim about the writer's rhetorical choices and their relationship to purpose or message, rather than restating the prompt, listing devices, or summarizing the passage.
cards.n: Row A is one point and takes one sentence: name the purpose and the kind of choices that serve it.

cards.q: Recall what each row of the AP Lang FRQ rubric awards.
cards.a: Row A: thesis, 1 point. Row B: evidence and commentary, 4 points. Row C: sophistication, 1 point. Six points total per essay.
cards.n: Row B is where essays are won or lost; four of the six points ride on specific evidence plus explanation.

cards.q: Explain what earns the sophistication point.
cards.a: A consistently vivid and persuasive style, or genuine engagement with complexity: situating the argument in a broader context, exploring tensions and implications, or explaining the significance of a rhetorical situation. It cannot be earned by a phrase.
cards.n: Sophistication is a whole-essay quality; tacking on a broader implications sentence at the end rarely earns it.

cards.q: Explain what distinguishes analysis from evaluation on the AP Lang rhetorical analysis question.
cards.a: Analysis explains how and why a writer's choices work on an audience to serve a purpose. Evaluation judges whether the writer succeeded or was right, which the prompt never asks for.
cards.h: → how it works vs whether it's right
cards.n: Praising or criticizing the writer's position earns nothing on Q2 - stay inside the text's effect on its audience.

cards.q: Identify the flaw: an essay states a speaker 'uses an anecdote, a rhetorical question, and parallelism' and then moves on.
cards.a: This is device-spotting, not analysis - it names techniques without explaining how any one of them functions on the audience or advances the writer's purpose.
cards.n: This is one of the most common Row B point-losers - a reader cannot credit analysis that never actually happened.

cards.q: Contrast a rhetorical analysis paragraph organized by device and one organized by the writer's argumentative move.
cards.a: Device-based organization walks through techniques one at a time with no throughline. Move-based organization groups whatever choices serve one stage of the writer's argument, producing a line of reasoning instead of a list.
cards.n: Move-based paragraphs read as analysis of an argument; device-based paragraphs read as a scavenger hunt.

cards.q: Decide the stronger commentary: 'This shows the senator is passionate,' or 'the short sentences quicken the pace to convey urgency.'
cards.a: The second is stronger: it names the choice, the effect, and the purpose it serves. The first is a vague label with no textual anchor and could describe almost any passage.
cards.h: → pick one, then what it supplies
cards.n: Any commentary that could be copy-pasted onto a different passage is too generic to earn Row B credit.
